p01.why: A 1920s wooden ryokan on the Matsukawa river, now a hostel, where the baths are fed by Ito's own hot spring and stay open through the night. You arrive after the Fuji drive, soak twice, and sit in the lounge with the other guests. Breakfast is next to the river before the Jogasaki sunrise.
p01.only: Already booked for Nov 18: 7-bed tatami dorm with onsen included, balance paid at the desk. Check-in closes 20:00 and there is no car park, so budget ¥500–1,000 for the coin lot 35 m away.
p01.vr: It is booked, it is the cheapest real onsen night of the trip, and it is the base for the Nov 19 dark-sky and sunrise window.
p01.tk: on the drive day, about 2 h by car from Fuji; 1 h 40 by Odoriko train otherwise
p01.ky: 3 h 30, Nozomi to Atami then Ito line

p02.why: A Sengokuhara ryokan with milky white sulphur water piped from Owakudani, a kaiseki dinner served in the room and futons laid out while you eat. It is the classic one-night ryokan ritual: check in at 15:00, bath at dusk, dinner, second bath, sleep.
p02.only: This was the splurge night that the Izu loop replaced; nothing was booked. If you want a kaiseki ryokan experience on a future trip, this is a fair mid-priced one (about ¥25,000–35,000 with dinner).
p02.vr: Dropped for K's House Ito, which is booked; re-adding it would mean losing the Izu coast and Jogasaki.
p02.tk: 2 h, Romancecar to Hakone-Yumoto then bus to Sengokuhara
p02.ky: 3 h, Nozomi to Odawara then bus

p03.why: A small island off the Shonan coast with a shrine climb, a botanical garden lighthouse, sea caves at the far end and seafood stalls on the way down. Late afternoon from the west cliffs you get Fuji over the water on a clear day. It is Tokyo's easy seaside half-day.
p03.only: The only sea-and-caves walk on your list, and the closest coast to Tokyo. But you already get the Pacific at Jogasaki on Nov 19, which is wilder and emptier.
p03.vr: 1 h each way from Shinjuku eats a full afternoon, and the Izu coast gives you a better version of it on the drive.
p03.tk: 1 h 10, Odakyu Romancecar to Katase-Enoshima or JR to Fujisawa
p03.ky: 3 h, Nozomi to Shin-Yokohama then local

p04.why: The river that links Asakusa to Skytree. The point is not a sight but a 25-minute walk along the terraces at golden hour, with Skytree reflected in the water and the Asahi flame across the bridge. From Nui Kuramae it is your front yard.
p04.only: Different from every other nature entry: it is a city walk, free, and on your doorstep for three nights. Not a destination, a route.
p04.vr: Costs nothing and replaces a metro ride between Asakusa and Skytree; the supermoon rises over it on Nov 24.

p05.why: A wild gorge in the Kiso mountains where the river runs an unreal emerald green over white granite. You walk the forest road along the valley, swim-spot to swim-spot, with nobody around. It is the kind of place that defines a summer road trip.
p05.only: The purest water on your list, more vivid than Mitarai Valley, but it is a summer and early-autumn place; by mid-November the leaves are down and the valley road closes to cars from early December.
p05.vr: Four-plus hours each way from Tokyo and past its season; Mitarai Valley on Nov 21 gives you the emerald-water feeling inside the plan.
p05.tk: 4 h, Shinkansen to Nagoya, Shinano express to Nojiri, then taxi

p06.why: A 58-hectare imperial garden ten minutes from the Shinjuku chaos, with a French lawn, an English lawn, a Japanese pond garden and a greenhouse. You walk slowly, sit, and reset after a shopping morning. The maples by the Japanese garden start turning in the last week of November.
p06.only: The biggest green space in central Tokyo and the calmest; unlike Meiji Jingu it is a landscape garden, not a shrine forest. ¥500, no alcohol, last entry 16:00.
p06.vr: A cheap decompression stop between Nakano and the Nov 17 evening; colour will be early-stage but the lawns and light are the point.

p07.why: A 300 m avenue of 146 ginkgo trees pruned into cones, running from Aoyama-dori to the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery. When it turns, the whole street is a yellow tunnel and the pavement is gold. In 2026 the Tokyo ginkgo peak is forecast around Nov 26, so on Nov 23–24 you will catch it just turning.
p07.only: The most famous ginkgo view in Tokyo, and the only one on your list that is a formal avenue rather than a park; Hachioji on Nov 18 is longer but wilder, Hongo campus is older and quieter.
p07.vr: Fifteen minutes of walking on a shopping day in Aoyama, free, and your last chance at autumn colour before the flight.

p08.why: A small Rinzai Zen temple in the Ichijoji hills with the most photographed framed maple view in Kyoto: you sit on the tatami and the garden is the picture. Behind it a bamboo path climbs to a view over the whole city. In autumn 2026 entry is by advance reservation, which caps the crowd.
p08.only: Unlike the big Higashiyama temples this is one room, one garden, one view. Shisen-do next door is the same mood, and Ichijoji ramen street is a 10-minute walk.
p08.vr: The Kyoto moment you came for, and the reservation system keeps it sane even on the three-day weekend; book on enkouji.jp as soon as the autumn slots open.
p08.tk: 2 h 50, Nozomi then Eizan line to Ichijoji
p08.ky: 35 min, Karasuma line to Matsugasaki then taxi, or bus 5

p09.why: Four kilometres of 770 ginkgo trees along the old Koshu-kaido highway from Oiwake-cho to Takao station in Hachioji, with the Ichō Matsuri street festival on Nov 21–22. You drive it on Nov 18 as the first stop of the MX-5 day: windows down, yellow on both sides.
p09.only: Your own note was the festival; the festival weekend clashes with Kyoto, so you get the avenue on a Wednesday without stalls but also without traffic. The longest ginkgo avenue on the list by far.
p09.vr: Already stop one of Day 3; it costs 15 minutes of detour off the Chuo expressway and Hachioji trees turn earlier than central Tokyo.
p09.tk: on the drive day; 50 min by car from Adachi, or 55 min by Chuo line special rapid

p10.why: One of Japan's three great gardens, built by the Maeda lords over two centuries: ponds, bridges, the Kotoji stone lantern and old pines held up with the yukitsuri snow ropes that go up from Nov 1. Late November is its best month, with maples at peak and night illumination most years.
p10.only: The only true daimyo stroll garden on your list; Kyoto temple gardens are smaller and more framed. Kanazawa itself is a Kyoto without the crowds.
p10.vr: Kanazawa is a two-night detour (2.5 h each way) that does not fit the nine nights; it is the headline of your next trip, with Toyama.
p10.ky: 2 h 15, Thunderbird to Tsuruga then Hokuriku Shinkansen

p11.why: Nara Park: 1,200 free-roaming deer that bow for crackers, Todai-ji's giant Buddha hall, Kasuga Taisha's lantern paths, and Nakatanidou's high-speed mochi pounding on the way back to the station. Half a day, flat, and the deer under autumn trees are the photo.
p11.only: Nothing else on the list has the animals-in-a-temple-city mix. It is on your Saturday car day as the return leg from Mitarai Valley, so you reach it at the golden-hour end of the day.
p11.vr: Deer plus Todai-ji is a once-in-a-trip combination and it is already placed on Nov 21 on the way back to Kyoto.
p11.ky: 45 min, Kintetsu express from Kyoto, or on the Nov 21 drive

p12.why: The former emperor's palace inside the wide gravel park of Kyoto Gyoen. The palace itself is a free walk-in tour of halls and gates; the park around it has big ginkgo and maples and almost nobody in it compared with the temples.
p12.only: Scale and emptiness: it is the one Kyoto heritage site where you can walk a kilometre without a crowd. It is formal courtyards rather than gardens, so it lacks Enkoji's intimacy.
p12.vr: Free and 20 minutes from Tozando, but on a two-day Kyoto it only fits if the Friday runs ahead of schedule.

p13.why: The Inner Shrine of Ise, the holiest site in Shinto, rebuilt from scratch every 20 years for 1,300 years. You cross the Uji bridge, wash in the Isuzu river, and walk a cedar forest to a fence you cannot pass. Oharai-machi outside is an Edo street of akafuku mochi and grilled Ise lobster.
p13.only: Nothing else on the list carries this weight; Kotai Jingu is the origin point of the shrines you will see everywhere. But it is a pilgrimage, not a sight: no building to enter, no colour, just forest and gravel.
p13.vr: Two hours each way from Kyoto would cost you the Nara mountain day; it deserves its own trip paired with Mie's coast.
p13.tk: 3 h 30, Nozomi to Nagoya then Kintetsu limited express
p13.ky: 2 h, Kintetsu limited express from Kyoto

p14.why: The bamboo grove path at Sagano, 400 m of green stems that creak in the wind, plus Tenryu-ji's garden at its mouth and the Togetsukyo bridge across the river. It is the Kyoto postcard, which is exactly the problem: by 10:00 it is a conveyor belt.
p14.only: The only bamboo on the list, and Arashiyama's river-and-mountain setting is real; but on a Friday in late November it is the most crowded spot in Kyoto. The far west end (Otagi Nenbutsuji, Adashino) is empty and better.
p14.vr: Fine if you are at the grove by 08:30 straight off the 09:12 train; otherwise Kurama to Kibune gives you forest without the crowd.
p14.tk: 2 h 45, Nozomi then JR Sagano line
p14.ky: 20 min, JR Sagano line to Saga-Arashiyama

p16.why: The lacquered red bridge at the entrance to the Nikko shrines, then Toshogu with its carved gates, then the Irohazaka hairpins up to Lake Chuzenji and Kegon falls. Nikko in late November has the town trees still coloured and the mountains already bare.
p16.only: The most ornate shrine complex in Japan, nothing like the restraint of Kyoto. Also the worst traffic on a holiday weekend in the Kanto area.
p16.vr: A full day two hours from Asakusa, and the Nov 21–23 holiday makes it a traffic jam; Hakone and Fuji already take the mountain slot.
p16.tk: 2 h, Tobu limited express from Asakusa

p17.why: A Sea of Japan city with the Tateyama mountains as a wall behind it, Toyama Bay's glass-clear seafood and the gateway to the Alpine Route and Kurobe gorge. Pinned, I assume, for the mountain-over-sea skyline.
p17.only: Four hours from Tokyo, and the Alpine Route shuts for winter at the end of November; the city alone does not justify the ride.
p17.vr: Out of range for this trip; pair it with Kanazawa on a future Hokuriku trip in May for the snow walls.

p18.why: One of the world's largest aquariums, built around a nine-metre-deep Pacific tank with whale sharks and manta rays that you spiral down past for an hour. Your note was 'Biggest Aquarium'. The ferris wheel next door does sunset over Osaka bay.
p18.only: The whale shark tank is the one thing here you cannot see in Tokyo. But Osaka was dropped from the plan, so this now sits two hours from Kyoto on a day that ends with a train home.
p18.vr: Only if Osaka comes back into the Sunday; otherwise a 2.5-hour round trip from Kyoto for an aquarium is a poor trade for Ohara.
p18.tk: 3 h 15, Nozomi to Shin-Osaka then Chuo line to Osakako
p18.ky: 1 h 15, Shinkansen or JR special rapid then Chuo line

p19.why: A castle town in the Nagano basin with the black-walled Matsumoto castle, the original 1590s keep you can climb inside, plus Nakamachi's storehouse street and soba. It is the gateway to Kamikochi and the Kiso valley.
p19.only: The only original castle keep on your list (Kanazawa's is reconstructed) and the best-looking one in Japan. Not reachable without giving up a Tokyo or Kyoto day.
p19.vr: 2.5 hours from Shinjuku on the Azusa; a Nagano trip (with Togakushi and Kiso, both on your list) is the obvious next-trip shape.
p19.tk: 2 h 40, Azusa limited express from Shinjuku

p20.why: North of Koenji station: vintage clothing on every corner, record shops, the Kitakore building's deranged fashion collective, and punk bars and izakaya that fill up at 19:00. The local, scruffier version of Shimokitazawa, five minutes further on the Chuo line.
p20.only: Cheaper and less curated than Shimokita, with more secondhand Japanese streetwear and more live-house energy. Pal arcade on the south side is the covered street; the north is the bars.
p20.vr: Two stops from Nakano, so it slots into the Nov 17 camera-and-vintage afternoon without a detour.

p21.why: A Showa-era temple town in far east Tokyo: the Taishakuten temple with carved wooden walls, the Tora-san film museum, a street of dango and senbei stalls, and the Yagiri ferry across the Edo river. Old Tokyo at walking pace.
p21.only: The slowest, most local district on the list; nothing to buy and nothing famous, which is the appeal. Shibamata is to Asakusa what Shimokita is to Shibuya.
p21.vr: 45 minutes from Ueno each way is a lot for your last two days when Kuramae, Kappabashi and Asakusa are at the door.

p22.why: The station you get off at for Fujiya Camera's used floors, Nakano Broadway's four levels of Mandarake, toys and watches, and the cheap izakaya arcade in between. It is the whole Nov 17 afternoon in one five-minute radius.
p22.only: Nakano is where you buy the Fujifilm; it is the used-camera capital of Tokyo and Broadway is the collectors' mall that Akihabara wishes it were.
p22.vr: The camera purchase lives here, and it is five minutes from Shinjuku on the Chuo line.

p23.why: A Meiji-era stroll garden around a pond with stepping stones across the water, carp, herons and famous stones collected from across Japan. It sits in Kiyosumi-Shirakawa, Tokyo's coffee-roaster district, 15 minutes from Kuramae.
p23.only: Smaller and quieter than Shinjuku Gyoen, and the stepping-stone pond is its own thing; the real reason to come is the coffee street around it.
p23.vr: ¥150, half an hour, and it pairs with KOFFEE MAMEYA on a Kuramae morning.

p24.why: The Maeda clan's castle next to Kenroku-en, rebuilt in timber with the original white-lead tiles; you walk the gatehouses and the long storehouse. Mostly it is the grounds and the view across to the garden.
p24.only: A reconstruction, so less than Matsumoto's original keep; it is the bonus to Kenroku-en, not a reason to go on its own.
p24.vr: Belongs to the Kanazawa trip that does not fit this itinerary.

p25.why: Japan's oldest and largest museum, in Ueno park. For you the point is the Honkan's sword rooms: national-treasure tachi and katana laid flat under light so you can read the hamon, plus armour and ukiyo-e. Two hours is enough if you go straight to those galleries.
p25.only: The best public display of real blades in the country, and the context for anything you buy at Tozando. Also open until 20:00 on Fridays and weekends.
p25.vr: ¥1,000 and 15 minutes from the Oedo antique market; it fits a Nov 23 afternoon once the market ends.

p26.why: A museum of antique European music boxes and automata next to Tenryu-ji, with hourly demonstrations where the staff wind up 19th-century machines and let them play. Your note was 'Music box museum'. Quiet, warm and strange.
p26.only: Nothing else like it on the list; a sit-down half hour away from the Arashiyama crowd. Small, so ¥1,000 is steep for 40 minutes.
p26.vr: Only worth it if you are already in Arashiyama and need to get off the main path for a while.

p28.why: A 90-minute non-verbal show in a 1928 art-deco building: four performers who are robots in a toy factory, doing mime, breakdance, juggling, magic and projection-mapped lighting, with no language at all. It is intimate, technically astonishing, and the audience is small.
p28.only: Kyoto-only; there is no equivalent in Tokyo. It is the one evening ticket in Kyoto that is worth paying for, and the only reason the Friday night is in the city rather than Ichijoji.
p28.vr: World-class and language-free, and it anchors the Friday evening; book online, back-row seats are fine and about ¥4,000.

p29.why: The graves of the 47 ronin inside Sengaku-ji, with incense still burning on each stone three centuries later. You buy a bundle at the gate, walk the rows, and look at the well where they washed Kira's head. Ten minutes from Shinagawa.
p29.only: Same site as Sengaku-ji on your shrine list, so rate them as one. It is the most direct contact with bushido on the list, and the small museum has the men's own letters and gear.
p29.vr: Free, 45 minutes, and on the way between Shinagawa and the city; the kind of place that lands harder when you know the story.
p29.tk: 15 min, Yamanote to Shinagawa then walk
p29.ky: 2 h 25, Nozomi to Shinagawa then walk

p30.why: A hillside sculpture park in Hakone with Henry Moore bronzes on the lawns, a Picasso pavilion, the stained-glass Symphonic Sculpture tower you climb inside, and a hot-spring foot bath at the bottom. Two hours in the open air with the mountains behind everything.
p30.only: The only art-in-landscape place on the list, and the best thing in Hakone that is not a bath. It needs a half-day you no longer have in Hakone.
p30.vr: The Nov 19 Hakone leg is already full with the Skyline, Turnpike and Amazake Chaya, and the car must be back by 18:30.
p30.tk: 1 h 50, Romancecar then Tozan railway to Chokoku-no-mori
p30.ky: 3 h, Nozomi to Odawara then Tozan

p31.why: The curved 3D screen above Shinjuku's east exit where a giant calico cat wakes, yawns and knocks things off the ledge between adverts. You stand across the road from the station, watch two loops, and film it. Thirty seconds of why-is-Tokyo-like-this.
p31.only: The purest cyberpunk-Tokyo moment on the list and it is free, 24 hours, and three minutes from UNPLAN; it is your first-night opener.
p31.vr: Costs nothing and sits on the walk to Omoide Yokocho; it is already Day 1's second stop.

p32.why: The steaming hot-spring field in the centre of Kusatsu Onsen, where 4,000 litres a minute of acidic water runs down wooden channels to cool, lit green at night. Around it: free public baths, the yumomi water-stirring show and a town of ryokan.
p32.only: The strongest spring water in Japan and the most atmospheric onsen town on the list; Ito and Hakone are milder in every sense.
p32.vr: 3.5 hours from Tokyo in the Gunma mountains; a two-night winter trip of its own.
p32.tk: 3 h 30, Shinkansen to Karuizawa then bus, or JR bus from Shinjuku
p32.ky: 5 h, Nozomi then Shinkansen then bus

p33.why: A road bridge in Fuji city whose line, from the right spot at the north end, appears to run straight up into Mount Fuji. It is a five-minute photo stop that went viral and is now a small tourist attraction with a car park and polite signs.
p33.only: A gimmick, but a good one, and it is 15 minutes from Obuchi Sasaba on the Nov 18 route. The shot works best in the hour before sunset, which is exactly when you pass.
p33.vr: Twenty minutes off the drive to Ito at the point in the day when the K's House 20:00 check-in starts to bite.
p33.tk: on the drive day, 15 min from the tea fields
p33.ky: 2 h 15, Shinkansen to Shin-Fuji then taxi

p34.why: 634 m tower with a 350 m deck and the 450 m Tembo Galleria ramp; at night the whole Kanto grid runs to the horizon and Fuji sits on it on clear days. From Nui Kuramae it is a 25-minute river walk.
p34.only: The highest view in Tokyo; Shibuya Sky is more fashionable but lower and more crowded. On Nov 24 the supermoon rises beside it, which is the better free show from the river.
p34.vr: Book the combo online (about ¥3,100) for a clear evening; if it is hazy, watch it from the Sumida instead and keep the money.

p35.why: Goldfish in kaleidoscopic tanks under coloured light on the ninth floor of Ginza Mitsukoshi: an Instagram installation that is genuinely pretty for 40 minutes. It is 15 minutes from the Oedo antique market.
p35.only: Closer to teamLab than to an aquarium; if you do teamLab Planets this is the same idea at a smaller scale and ¥2,500 to 2,700 is a lot for it.
p35.vr: Only if the Nov 23 afternoon has a hole after the market and you skip teamLab; otherwise redundant.

p36.why: Nagoya-style tebasaki chicken wings, fried twice, glazed sweet-soy and buried in pepper and sesame, in a loud counter joint in Amemura. Your note: 'Peak Wings'. Beer, wings, more wings. Open until 02:00.
p36.only: The wings are the real Nagoya style and Amemura is Osaka's streetwear district, so it pairs with Triangle Park and the thrift shops. But Osaka is out of the plan; the chain's nearest Tokyo-area equivalent is Sekai no Yamachan, which is fine, not peak.
p36.vr: Only if Osaka returns to the Sunday evening; not worth a train ride from Kyoto on its own.
p36.tk: 3 h, Nozomi to Shin-Osaka then Midosuji line
p36.ky: 50 min, Shinkansen or special rapid then Midosuji line to Shinsaibashi

p37.why: A ten-seat omakase counter in Nishi-Azabu where the chef is relaxed, speaks English and adjusts the course to you. Your note: 'Top sushi'. About 20 pieces over two hours, ¥20,000 to 30,000. This is the splurge dinner if you take one.
p37.only: Among top-tier omakase this is one of the few that is bookable from abroad and welcomes first-timers; tell them you prefer lighter, non-fishy nigiri and they will steer. Better fish exists (Saito, Sugita) but you cannot get in.
p37.vr: Worth it once in a lifetime; book now through the restaurant or Omakase.in for Nov 17 or Nov 24, and only if the camera budget survives.
p37.tk: 25 min, Hibiya line to Roppongi then walk

p38.why: Fukuoka's famous mentaiko (spicy cod roe) baguette bakery in Hakata: a crisp French loaf with the roe and butter baked in, eaten warm from the bag. Fukuoka's whole food scene (tonkotsu, yatai stalls) is around it.
p38.only: The real thing exists only in Fukuoka, but Tokyo Station's Gransta has the same bakery's mentai france (sold out by noon most days), so you can taste it without Kyushu.
p38.vr: Fukuoka is 1,000 km off the route; grab the Tokyo Station branch's loaf before the Nov 20 Shinkansen instead.

p39.why: A tiny old-school yakiniku counter in Akasaka that only opens for weekday lunch (09:00 to 16:00, closed Tuesday and weekends). Your note: 'Best yakiniku'. You grill your own cuts on a tabletop burner and finish with the rice set.
p39.only: The hours make it a lunch-only hunt; Nov 17 (Tuesday) is closed, so it is Nov 23 if the holiday does not shut it, or Nov 24. Confirm by phone or Tabelog the day before. For an easier yakiniku, Yoroniku or any Jojoen branch is bookable and open evenings.
p39.vr: The hours fight your schedule; if a Nov 24 lunch in Akasaka works it is a great cheap meal, otherwise let it go.

p40.why: Japan's biggest curry chain, Shibuya branch: thick Japanese curry with a cutlet, spice levels 1 to 10, ¥1,000, no waiting, open to 23:00. The comfort refuel when you have walked all day and want something that tastes like home-adjacent.
p40.only: CoCo Ichi is everywhere, so there is nothing special about this branch except that it is in Shibuya. If you want curry that is actually special, Jimbocho's Bondy or Kyoeido on your p95 list beat it by a mile.
p40.vr: A fallback, not a destination; go when hungry near Shibuya, otherwise eat curry in Jimbocho where it means something.

p41.why: Conveyor-belt sushi where there is no belt: you order on a tablet and plates shoot to your seat on a bullet-train rail. ¥130 to 200 a plate, tamago, inari, corn mayo, chicken and whatever fish you feel like, ¥1,500 for a full meal. Shibuya Dogenzaka, late and loud.
p41.only: The most fun cheap sushi in Tokyo and a good first-sushi test if raw fish is not your thing; non-fish plates are half the menu. Genki Sushi is the same chain under another name.
p41.vr: Cheap, quick, central and a Tokyo story; fits any Shibuya evening on Nov 23 or 24.

p42.why: A small Neapolitan pizzeria in Gotanda with a wood oven and a lunch set around ¥1,500. Your note: 'V good pizza'. Closed Monday and Tuesday, lunch to 14:00 and dinner to 21:00.
p42.only: One of your five Tokyo pizza pins; the dough is good but Gotanda is off your route. Seirinkan is the icon and sits two stops from Shibuya, and pizza marumo is the one people queue for now.
p42.vr: Pick one or two pizzas for the trip, and Gotanda loses to Nakameguro and Ebisu on location.
p42.ky: 2 h 40, Nozomi to Shinagawa then Yamanote

p43.why: A relaxed Neapolitan pizzeria in Musashi-Koyama, 15 minutes' walk from Togoshi Ginza shopping street. Your note: 'V good pizza'. Open every day for lunch and dinner, which is rarer than it sounds.
p43.only: The pizza is solid rather than special; its real value is that it pairs with the Togoshi Ginza walk and is open seven days. Carlino's is better, Seirinkan more famous.
p43.vr: Only as the meal on a Togoshi Ginza afternoon; not worth a trip for itself.

p44.why: A tiny basement pizzeria in Nakameguro run by one pizzaiolo, lunch only on most days, with the highest rating of your pizza pins. Your note: 'Best pizza'. It sells out; arrive at opening.
p44.only: The best dough on the list by reputation, and 10 minutes' walk from Seirinkan, so you can compare the two in one afternoon. Odd hours (closed Monday and Thursday, lunch only) make it a plan-around.
p44.vr: If one pizza is special on the trip, this is it; a Nov 24 lunch in Nakameguro, then thrift along the canal.

p45.why: A lunch-only pizzeria in Kagurazaka, the French-Japanese lane of stone steps and bistros behind Iidabashi. Your note: 'Pizza'. Pizza by the slice or whole pies until 18:00.
p45.only: Kagurazaka itself is the attraction; the pizza is a reason to wander it. Seirinkan and Carlino's are better pizza, Kagurazaka is a better street.
p45.vr: A nice lunch if a Nov 23 or 24 morning ends near Iidabashi, otherwise skip.

p46.why: The pizzeria that started Tokyo's Neapolitan scene, in a strange multi-floor Nakameguro building with a wood oven at the bottom. Two pizzas only: margherita and marinara. You eat, you leave, you understand why Tokyo pizza is a thing.
p46.only: The original and the easiest to fit: two stops from Shibuya, open every day, no reservation. Carlino's dough is better now, but Seirinkan is the one you tell people about.
p46.vr: The pizza stop that fits the plan without planning; Nov 24 lunch before Nakameguro thrift.

p47.why: A 1.3 km covered-and-open shotengai in Shinagawa ward: 400 shops of croquettes, oden, yakitori, grocers and old-school cafés, with locals doing their evening shopping. Your note: 'Local street'. You graze your way down it.
p47.only: Longer and more ordinary than Ameyoko, which is the point: this is where Tokyo actually shops. Togoshi Ginza croquettes are the thing to eat.
p47.vr: A good 90 minutes but 20 minutes off the Shibuya axis; Jujo Ginza and Ameyoko cover the same ground closer to your bases.

p48.why: The kaiseki restaurant that sits at the top of Tabelog's national ranking: an eight-seat counter in Shinbashi, one seating, about ¥40,000 a head, booked months out by regulars. Your note: 'tabelog #1'.
p48.only: There is no Tokyo meal more coveted and almost no way in from abroad; a hotel concierge at a luxury hotel might manage it with weeks of notice. Shinjuku Kappo Nakajima (lunch, ¥1,000, Michelin star) is the sane alternative for seeing kaiseki technique.
p48.vr: Unbookable in practice and over the whole food budget; keep it as the dream.

p49.why: The Roppongi Hard Rock Cafe: burgers, ribs, the Tokyo pin and the city T-shirt. It is the same restaurant it is in Bengaluru, with a different pin.
p49.only: Nothing you cannot get anywhere else except the Tokyo merch; if you collect the pins, buy the pin and eat elsewhere. Roppongi itself is worth it for teamLab Borderless.
p49.vr: A chain meal in a city with the best food in the world; grab the pin at the shop counter if you must and keep the evening.

p50.why: A standing counter at Tsukiji outer market, open from 06:30, famous for its horumon-don (simmered offal over rice) and a straightforward gyudon. Cash only, you eat on the pavement with the market crowd. Open Monday, Tuesday, Thursday to Saturday until 13:00.
p50.only: The gyudon here is miso-simmered and nothing like Yoshinoya; it is the real breakfast of the market. Tsukiji's outer market is still the best grazing street in Tokyo despite the fish auction moving to Toyosu.
p50.vr: A ¥1,000 07:00 breakfast on Nov 23 before the antique market, five minutes away; the hours rule out Sunday and Wednesday.

p51.why: The pizzeria Tokyo is queueing for right now, in Ebisu: a Tokyo-style take on Neapolitan with a lighter crust, inventive toppings and a wine list. Expect a 30 to 60 minute wait at lunch or a hard-to-get dinner booking.
p51.only: The only pizza pin that is a scene rather than a shrine; Seirinkan is history, marumo is now. If you only do one pizza and want the one with buzz, this is it.
p51.vr: One stop from Shibuya and open seven days; take it for Nov 23 dinner if Seirinkan goes to lunch.

p52.why: A counter in Namba for wagyu burgers and steak, five minutes from Dotonbori. Your note: 'Burger'. Lunch sets around ¥2,000, dinner steaks more. Osaka's cheap-and-loud food district is on the doorstep.
p52.only: Osaka is out of the current plan; for a wagyu burger in Tokyo, Blacows in Ebisu or Shogun Burger near Shinjuku do the same thing closer to your bed.
p52.vr: Only if the Sunday ends in Osaka; otherwise not worth a train from Kyoto.
p52.tk: 3 h, Nozomi then Midosuji line to Namba
p52.ky: 55 min, Shinkansen or special rapid then Midosuji line

p53.why: A late-night ramen counter in Sapporo's Susukino, in a ramen alley, serving the thick miso ramen Hokkaido invented. Open 19:00 to 02:00, closed Monday. It is on your list because the rating is 4.9.
p53.only: Sapporo is a two-hour flight away. The closest you get to this bowl in Tokyo is Sumire in Shinjuku or Ramen Street at Tokyo Station, both of which serve real Sapporo miso ramen.
p53.vr: Hokkaido is a separate trip; eat miso ramen at Tokyo Station's Ramen Street on the way to the Nov 20 train.
p53.tk: 4 h, flight from Haneda plus transfers
p53.ky: 5 h, flight from Itami plus transfers

p54.why: Walk through the Kaminarimon lantern, down Nakamise's 90 snack stalls, to the incense cauldron and the main hall, then pull an omikuji fortune for ¥100. It is the one Tokyo temple that still feels like a festival every day, and it sits five minutes from your Kuramae hostel.
p54.only: The oldest temple in Tokyo (645 AD) and the only one with a full market street as its approach; everything else in the Asakusa plan (Kappabashi, Bunkoya, the underground arcade) radiates from here.
p54.vr: Free, next to your bed for three nights, and the five-storey pagoda lit at night is a ten-minute stroll after dinner; go at 07:00 or after 20:00 to have it without the crowds.

p55.why: The vermilion shrine at the top of Shijo street is open all night and lit by hundreds of lanterns, so it works as the end of a Gion evening rather than a daytime stop. Walk in from Hanamikoji, pass through to Maruyama Park, and come back down Shirakawa canal lane.
p55.only: Unlike Kyoto's paid temples it never closes and costs nothing; the lantern hall after dark is the best free night photo in the city.
p55.vr: Worth 30 minutes on the Friday evening after GEAR, because it is on the way; skip it in daytime on the three-day weekend when Gion is a crush.
p55.ky: 20 min, bus 206 or Keihan to Gion-Shijo

p56.why: A small neighbourhood shrine in Tawaramoto, a farming town between Nara and the Yoshino mountains, with three Google reviews and no tourist layer at all. You would stand in a quiet precinct with a torii, a stone lion pair and nobody else.
p56.only: The only place on your list that is purely local; the appeal is the emptiness, not the building.
p56.vr: A 40-minute detour on the Saturday drive back from Mitarai Valley; only worth it if the name means something to you, otherwise Kasuga Taisha in Nara gives the same quiet with more to see.
p56.ky: 1 h 15 by car, or 1 h Kintetsu to Tawaramoto

p57.why: The Great Buddha hall is the largest wooden building you will ever stand inside, and the 15 m bronze Buddha fills it. Deer bow for crackers at the gate, and the climb to Nigatsu-do's wooden balcony behind the hall gives the view over Nara's roofs at sunset.
p57.only: Scale is the point: nothing in Kyoto is this big. It pairs with Kasuga Taisha's 3,000 lanterns on a single forest walk.
p57.vr: If you drive through Nara on the Saturday it is the one paid stop to make; arrive by 16:00 so the Nigatsu-do balcony catches the light.
p57.ky: 50 min, Kintetsu to Nara + 20 min walk; 1 h by car

p58.why: This is the Saihoji in Suginami, a small temple a short walk from Koenji, not the moss temple of Kyoto. You would see a modest gate, a cemetery and a quiet courtyard, nothing more.
p58.only: Almost certainly a pin for the wrong Saihoji; the Kyoto Kokedera needs a reservation months ahead and is not on this trip.
p58.vr: Nothing to see that Koenji's own streets do not give you; drop it unless you confirm it was a deliberate pick.
p58.tk: 25 min, Chuo line to Koenji + 10 min walk

p59.why: The temple where the 47 ronin are buried next to their lord, with incense still burning on every grave and a small museum of their armour and letters. Thirty minutes covers the graves, the well where the head was washed, and the museum.
p59.only: The Graveyard of the 47 Ronin on your list is this same site, so rate them together; the story is the attraction, and it is a sword story.
p59.vr: Ten minutes from Shinagawa, so it fits on the way to or from Haneda or a Nov 24 afternoon; closes at 16:00, so it cannot be an evening stop.
p59.tk: 15 min, Yamanote to Shinagawa + 10 min walk

p60.why: Three hundred stalls of household clear-outs in the Oi Racecourse car park: cameras, denim, tools, ceramics, old toys, and prices that drop with a smile. Haggling is expected and most sellers are families, not dealers.
p60.only: The biggest flea market in Tokyo and the cheapest; the Oedo Antique Market is classier and pricier, this one is where ¥500 finds happen.
p60.vr: It runs on the Sat–Sun you are in Kansai (Nov 21–22); on the holiday Monday Nov 23 it closes at 13:30, which collides with the Oedo market, so it only works if you catch the 06:00 train back.
p60.tk: 25 min, Keikyu to Tachiaigawa + 10 min walk

p61.why: Six floors of used cameras graded on a strict scale, each with a one-year warranty and a price that matches the website. You can handle a Fujifilm X-T20 and X-E3 side by side, then walk out with the one that feels right.
p61.only: The widest used-Fujifilm stock in Japan under one roof and the only big used dealer with a full year's warranty; Fujiya in Nakano is usually a little cheaper, so check both before paying.
p61.vr: Use it as the price check and the fallback if Fujiya has sold the body you want; it is five minutes from your Shinjuku hostel so it costs nothing to look.
p61.tk: 15 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku + 5 min walk

p62.why: A two-floor shop of original Japanese release posters, lobby cards and film magazines from the 1950s onward, sorted by title. Kurosawa, Godzilla and the Japanese printing of Blade Runner all turn up, and a B2 poster rolls into a tube that fits your bag.
p62.only: The one specialist in Jimbocho for movie paper; most of the other 170 shops are books. Prices run from about ¥1,500 for a lobby card to tens of thousands for a first-run classic.
p62.vr: Fits the same afternoon as Jimbocho Book Town and the Akihabara walk; closes 18:30 on weekdays, 18:00 on Saturday, so keep it before Akihabara, not after.
p62.tk: 10 min, Mita or Hanzomon line to Jimbocho

p63.why: A 1955 underground passage under Asakusa station with fortune tellers, a barber, standing bars and three or four cheap Thai and Vietnamese counters. Ten minutes of walking through it is the point; a bowl of pho there is a bonus.
p63.only: Tokyo's oldest underground arcade and still unrestored, which no other place on your list is. For a real meal, Asakusa's street food above ground beats it.
p63.vr: You will pass the entrance every day you use Asakusa station from Kuramae, so give it ten minutes once rather than planning around it.
p63.cuisine: Showa standing bars, Thai and Vietnamese counters

p64.why: The Nakano used-camera shop that pros and students both trust: honestly graded bodies in the main store, lenses in the annex across the lane, and staff who will let you mount a lens and shoot test frames. This is where your Fujifilm comes from.
p64.only: Consistently the lowest used prices in Tokyo for Fujifilm X bodies and the best grading accuracy; Map Camera has the warranty, Fujiya has the price. Next door to Nakano Broadway.
p64.vr: The camera is the one purchase the whole trip's photos depend on, and Nov 17 is early enough to shoot everything after; a used X-T20 or X-E3 kit sits around ¥60,000 to 90,000.
p64.tk: 15 min, Chuo line to Nakano + 5 min walk

p65.why: Tozando's Shogoin shop stocks iaito practice swords, bokken, shinai, kendo armour and some antique blades, with English-speaking staff who let you draw a sword and feel the balance. It sits five minutes from Heian Shrine, so it slots into a Kyoto afternoon.
p65.only: The only sword shop on the trip where you can handle real iaito and get export paperwork done for you; Tokyo has Seiyudo and Japan Sword for antiques, but nobody else ships a practice sword for you. A bokken (¥3,000 to 8,000) is the paperwork-free buy.
p65.vr: This is your interest, it is on the Friday afternoon, and it is the right place to decide between bokken, iaito and replica tanto before committing to the Indian import rules.

p66.why: Honcho-dori is a straight Showa-era shopping street with Mount Fuji filling the end of it, which is why it is in every Japan photo feed. The shops are half-shuttered but the signage, the overhead wires and the mountain make the frame.
p66.only: The only place where Fuji appears as a street backdrop rather than behind a lake or a pagoda; two minutes from Yoshida udon and ten from the Chureito pagoda, so it is three Fuji shots in an hour.
p66.vr: It is already on the Wednesday drive and costs nothing but ten minutes; mornings with clear air are best, and you will be there by late morning.
p66.tk: 2 h by car on the drive day; 2 h 15 by Fujikyu bus

p67.why: A long covered shotengai in Kita ward where locals buy croquettes, fish and ¥100 vegetables, with a few standing bars at the Jujo station end. You walk it in 20 minutes, eat a menchi-katsu from a window and keep going.
p67.only: Cheaper and less photographed than Togoshi Ginza, and close to the Akabane standing-bar streets if you want a salaryman night; nothing to buy that Ameyoko does not also have.
p67.vr: Only if a Tokyo evening is empty and you want a non-tourist street; Ameyoko and Togoshi are on routes you already take.

p68.why: The Shibuya Mandarake is one big basement of manga, figures, cels and retro games, with a glass case of the rare carts. It is where you check whether an LSD Dream Emulator or a boxed Game Boy turns up at a price you can live with.
p68.only: The Shibuya branch is smaller but calmer than the Nakano complex and keeps its best games in one place; Nakano has 20 shops but spreads them out. Super Potato in Akihabara has more consoles.
p68.vr: Pair it with Tower Records and the Shibuya evening; if you already combed Nakano Broadway on Nov 17 this is a 30-minute second look, not a destination.

p69.why: Low-rise lanes of vintage shops, record stores (Flash Disc Ranch, Jet Set, Disk Union), curry houses and tiny theatres, all walkable from one station. The afternoon is browsing with no plan, then a soup curry and a beer.
p69.only: The vinyl density is the draw: no other district on the list has three serious record shops within five minutes of each other. Koenji is its scruffier, cheaper cousin.
p69.vr: It is your 'vinyl, old Tokyo' note made real and is already on Nov 17 after Nakano; shops open at noon, so it is an afternoon, not a morning.
p69.tk: 25 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku + Odakyu 8 min

p70.why: A small, friendly knife shop in Kappabashi with English-speaking staff, a wall of gyuto, santoku and petty knives from Seki and Sakai makers, and free name engraving while you wait. You can hold ten knives before choosing.
p70.only: The best beginner-friendly service on the street; Kama-Asa two minutes away has a wider, more serious range and Tsubaya has the pro stock, so look at all three before paying. Knives fly in checked baggage with no paperwork.
p70.vr: A knife is the single most useful souvenir of the trip and this is on the Nov 24 Asakusa morning; budget ¥15,000 to 30,000 for a 210 mm gyuto.
p70.tk: 25 min, Ginza line to Tawaramachi + 8 min walk

p71.why: An 800 m street of restaurant-supply shops: knives, pots, ceramics by the kilo, noren curtains, bamboo steamers, and the plastic food models that cost more than a real meal. You walk it end to end, buying the cheap useful things you did not know you wanted.
p71.only: The ceramics and tea-pot prices here are the lowest in Tokyo because it sells to restaurants; nowhere else on the list combines knives and tableware in one street.
p71.vr: Most shops close on Sunday and many on the Nov 23 holiday, so it has to be the Tuesday Nov 24 morning, which is where it already sits.
p71.tk: 25 min, Ginza line to Tawaramachi + 5 min walk

p72.why: A warehouse-sized Book Off in Omiya with used games, watches, brand clothes, instruments and tools under one roof, all priced to clear. It is the suburban version of the thrift hunt, with more stock and fewer tourists than any Tokyo branch.
p72.only: The scale and the clothes are what Tokyo's Book Offs lack; for games alone, Super Potato and Mandarake are better curated.
p72.vr: Forty minutes each way for a half day of browsing you can mostly do in Nakano and Akihabara; only if the Nov 24 free day stays empty.

p73.why: A 1966 shopping complex that became the Mandarake mothership: twenty specialist shops across four floors for retro consoles, cels, figures, vintage watches and doujinshi, plus a ¥500 soft-serve stacked eight flavours high. Fujiya Camera is at the door.
p73.only: The only place in Japan where retro games, vintage Seikos and anime cels are each sold by their own specialist shop in one building; Mandarake Galaxy on the 4th floor is where the boxed rarities are.
p73.vr: It is where the camera day happens, two or three hours disappear here easily, and it is on Nov 17 already.
p73.tk: 15 min, Chuo line to Nakano + 5 min walk

p74.why: The electronics district: arcades on every corner, Super Potato's retro floors, Yodobashi's keyboard aisle, gachapon halls and the parts arcade under the tracks. One long afternoon into the evening, when the neon comes on, covers it.
p74.only: Nothing else on the list has the arcade and retro-game density; Nakano is for buying, Akihabara is for playing. GTA 6 ships Nov 19, so the game floors will be loud that weekend.
p74.vr: Your cyberpunk brief and your keyboard shopping both land here; it is on Nov 23, and the holiday crowd is part of the show.

p75.why: A market street under the Yamanote tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi: dried fish, Calbee stands, ¥1,000 sneakers, knock-off fragrances and standing bars that fill with salarymen by 17:00. Walk it, snack, and finish at a tachinomi.
p75.only: The only Tokyo street where a market, a snack run and a drinking session are the same 300 m; Jujo and Togoshi are quieter but have no bars like Takioka.
p75.vr: It is the natural end of the Nov 23 Akihabara afternoon (10 min walk) and the start of the salaryman night; nothing to buy that justifies a separate trip.

p76.why: Nine floors of everything electronic, with the keyboard corner (HHKB, Realforce, Keychron) where you can type on every switch, a Casio and G-Shock wall, Tamagotchis, and the game floor with PS5 demo units. Tax-free counter on every floor.
p76.only: The only shop where you can try a Happy Hacking and a Realforce side by side before buying; Akihabara's small keyboard shops (Yushakobo) are for custom builds, this is for finished boards and Japanese-layout stock.
p76.vr: Buy the keyboard here on Nov 23; from Nov 1 the tax refund is paid at the airport, so keep every receipt and allow 20 minutes at Narita.

p77.why: The 52nd-floor bar of the Park Hyatt from Lost in Translation: floor-to-ceiling glass over Shinjuku, a live jazz trio from 20:00, cocktails from ¥2,500. One drink, one hour, the whole city lit beneath you.
p77.only: The best night view on the list that you can sit down in, and the only bar with a film attached; the cover charge (¥2,500 to 3,000) kicks in at 20:00 unless you are inside already.
p77.vr: Worth one expensive drink on Nov 17 if you want the cityscape from inside; Benfiddich is the better cocktail, this is the better room. Dress smart-casual.
p77.tk: 20 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku + 12 min walk or free hotel shuttle

p78.why: A bar the width of a corridor inside Omoide Yokocho, three floors, red walls, chandeliers, and a ¥500 seat charge that buys you a stool shoulder to shoulder with strangers. Drinks are ¥700 to 900 and the room is the show.
p78.only: The one bar in the yakitori alley that is actually a bar; Golden Gai has 200 similar rooms but Albatross is the easiest first one, no cover tricks, English menu.
p78.vr: First night, five minutes from your hostel, cheap, and a perfect first-night Japan room; it is already on Nov 16.
p78.tk: 20 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku + 3 min walk

p80.why: From this tiny station on the Ome line you walk down to Hatonosu Gorge: a green river between cliffs, a suspension bridge, and a cliff-side cafe with a terrace over the water. Two hours of walking in real mountain air inside Tokyo prefecture.
p80.only: The closest deep-gorge nature to central Tokyo, and the last foliage of your trip (Okutama peaks around Nov 20–25); Mitarai in Nara is the bigger version with brighter water, Atera is the far-away version.
p80.vr: A three-to-four hour round trip that only makes sense as a Nov 24 free-day escape; you already get bigger nature on the drive days and in Nara.

p81.why: The smallest Fuji lake, with a free north-shore lot and a shoreline where Fuji sits directly across the water with almost nobody around. Ten minutes of standing still, a few frames, and back in the car.
p81.only: Of the five lakes this is the one with no tour buses and the cleanest reflection; Kawaguchiko has the shops and the crowds, Motosu has the ¥1,000-note view.
p81.vr: It is a ten-minute detour on the Wednesday drive between Fujiyoshida and Motosu, so take it; the reflection is best before noon when the wind drops.
p81.tk: 2 h 15 by car on the drive day

p82.why: Mitarai Valley is a 3 km gorge path with suspension bridges over water so clear and green it looks lit from below, with waterfalls at every bend. It is your 'beautiful water' note and the most dramatic nature on the trip's Kansai days.
p82.only: No other place on your list has water this colour; Hatonosu and Atera are the Kanto and Kiso versions, both smaller. The maples here are past peak by Nov 21, but the water does not care.
p82.vr: It is the reason the Saturday car day exists and it is empty while Kyoto is at its worst; two hours in the gorge, then a soak at Dorogawa Onsen next door.
p82.tk: 5 h by car via the Tomei
p82.ky: 2 h by car via the Keinawa and Route 309

p83.why: Katsunuma is the wine valley on the north side of the Misaka mountains, with thirty wineries along one road and tasting rooms that pour the local Koshu white for a few hundred yen. The grape harvest is over by November, but the cellars and the shinshu (new-vintage) tastings are open.
p83.only: Japan's only real wine region within reach of Tokyo and a different kind of countryside from the lakes; it is an alternative end to the Fuji loop, not an addition to it.
p83.vr: You are driving a manual sports car on that day, so a wine valley is the wrong detour; the tea fields at Obuchi Sasaba give the same farm-country feeling with no drink involved.
p83.tk: 1 h 30, Chuo line limited express to Katsunuma-budokyo

p84.why: The teamLab that makes you take your shoes off: knee-deep water with koi projected on it, a mirrored infinity room of hanging flowers, a garden of floating orchids. Ninety minutes, barefoot, in the dark, and it is as good as the photos.
p84.only: Planets is the body-in-the-work one; Borderless at Azabudai is bigger and more cerebral, and Biovortex in Kyoto is the newest. Do one of the three, not all.
p84.vr: The Nov 18 08:00 slot before picking up the car works if you want it, but it costs ¥3,800 to 4,800 and a dark room at 08:00 is a strange way to start a sunrise-to-sunset drive day; Biovortex in Kyoto is the fresher option if you only do one.
p84.tk: 25 min, Yurakucho line + Yurikamome to Shin-Toyosu

p85.why: A small Asakusa leather workshop that embroiders kawaii motifs and traditional patterns onto wallets, coin purses and card cases, made in-house since 1914. You pick a motif and a colour and walk out with a wallet nobody back home will have.
p85.only: Bunkoya makes the Bunko-gawa embroidered leather that other shops only resell; the Asakusa store has the fullest range and the lowest prices for it. A coin purse starts around ¥3,000, a long wallet ¥15,000+.
p85.vr: Two minutes from Senso-ji on the Nov 24 morning, so it is a free stop; the only question is whether a ¥10,000 wallet is on your list.

p86.why: Thrift sold by the kilo in a converted public bathhouse: you fill a bag from racks of American and Japanese vintage and pay by weight, usually ¥1,500 to 4,000 per kilo depending on the rack. The tiled bath walls are still there.
p86.only: The only by-weight thrift on your list, and the quirkiest building; Shimokitazawa's other vintage shops (Flamingo, Chicago) are curated and priced per piece. New York Joe Exchange next door also buys your old clothes.
p86.vr: It is inside the Nov 17 Shimokitazawa afternoon already; give it 30 minutes and buy only what fits your 25 kg allowance.
p86.tk: 25 min, Chuo line + Odakyu to Shimokitazawa

p87.why: The two-storey 1950s arcade under the Akihabara tracks where the district began: fifty closet-sized stalls of resistors, vacuum tubes, LEDs, switches, military radios and one shop that only sells wire. You walk the narrow aisles and buy a ¥300 switch you do not need.
p87.only: The last of the original parts bazaar, and the only place to see the pre-anime Akihabara; nothing like it in Nakano or Shibuya.
p87.vr: Fifteen minutes at the start of the Nov 23 Akihabara afternoon, right at the station; it closes at 19:00, so do it first.

p88.why: The pin sits in Okuwa village in the Kiso valley, the mountain corridor of the old Nakasendo road: cedar forests, the emerald Kiso river, and the Edo post towns of Tsumago and Magome an hour south. The classic day is the 8 km forest walk between the two towns.
p88.only: The only place on your list that is old-road Japan rather than temple Japan: wooden post towns with no wires, almost empty in late November. Atera Valley on your list is the same village, so they are one trip.
p88.vr: Three and a half hours each way from Tokyo or two and a half from Kyoto, so it only works as a replacement for a Kyoto day, not an addition; foliage is over by then but the forest walk is best empty.
p88.tk: 3 h 30, Nozomi to Nagoya + Shinano express to Nojiri
p88.ky: 2 h 30, Shinkansen to Nagoya + Shinano express

p89.why: A 2 km straight avenue of 400-year-old cedars, 40 m tall, leading through a thatched gate to Togakushi's inner shrine at the foot of a cliff. You walk it slowly in near silence, then eat Togakushi soba in the village.
p89.only: The most serene single walk on your entire list, more than any Kyoto temple; late November means mist or the first snow, which makes it better, not worse. It is in Nagano, 1.5 h from Tokyo by Shinkansen plus a bus.
p89.vr: If you ever decide the Kyoto weekend is too crowded, this plus the snow monkeys and Zenkoji is the swap; as an add-on to the current plan it does not fit.
p89.tk: 2 h 45, Hokuriku Shinkansen to Nagano + bus 70 min
p89.ky: 4 h 30, Shinkansen via Nagoya + Shinano express + bus

p90.why: The University of Tokyo's Hongo campus has a double row of ginkgo trees along its main avenue that turns solid gold in the last week of November, framed by the red-brick Yasuda Auditorium. You walk in through the Aka-mon gate, nobody checks, and it is free.
p90.only: The ginkgo avenue that peaks when you are actually in Tokyo (Nov 23–25), unlike Meiji Jingu Gaien which may be a week early; it is also quieter than Gaien and has the old campus buildings as a backdrop.
p90.vr: A 40-minute stop that fits the Nov 24 free day between Jimbocho and Ueno, and it is the surest gold-leaf shot of the trip.

p91.why: The Philosopher's Path is a 2 km canal-side walk under maples and cherries from Ginkaku-ji south to Nanzen-ji, with small temples and coffee stands along the way. In the last ten days of November the maples here are usually at their best.
p91.only: The one Kyoto walk where foliage, water and temples line up in sequence; Enkoji and Shisen-do nearby are the sit-down versions, this is the walking version. Eikando's lit maples are at its southern end.
p91.vr: Worth it on the Sunday morning before Ohara if you start by 08:00; by 10:00 on the three-day weekend it is a queue.

p92.why: An airsoft shooting range on the 8th floor of Marui Men in Shinjuku: you rent a pistol or rifle replica, get a lane and a paper target, and shoot BBs for 30 or 60 minutes. Staff explain everything and it is a legal, indoor version of something you cannot do at home.
p92.only: The only place on your list where you handle replica firearms; it is a game, not a gun club, and about ¥2,000 to 3,500 per session with rental included.
p92.vr: A fun 45 minutes if a Shinjuku evening has a gap, and it is five minutes from UNPLAN; it will not be something you remember over the sword cutting at HiSUi.
p92.tk: 20 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku + 5 min walk

p93.why: The convenience store opposite Kawaguchiko town hall with Mount Fuji rising directly over its blue sign: the photo that went viral enough for the town to put up a screen in 2024. The screen has since come down with rules and a guard, so the shot is possible again if you behave.
p93.only: Pure internet-era Japan and your 'My Fuji Lawson' note; it takes five minutes and a coffee. Fujiyoshida's Honcho street is the older, better version of the same idea.
p93.vr: It is a ten-minute detour from Oishi Park on the Wednesday drive and costs nothing; do it quickly, shoot from the marked spot, and do not cross the road.
p93.tk: 2 h by car on the drive day; 2 h Fujikyu bus to Kawaguchiko

p94.why: A family-run ryokan in Yanaka, the old temple district north of Ueno, with tatami rooms, a shared cypress bath and owners who have hosted foreigners since 1982. Nights run about ¥6,000 to 9,000 per person without meals.
p94.only: The only traditional Tokyo stay on your list and the only one in Yanaka, which is the most village-like part of central Tokyo; Nui in Kuramae is the social hostel alternative you already have.
p94.vr: Only if you decide the three Kuramae nights should be two and one night of tatami; otherwise K's House Ito already gives you the ryokan night.
p94.tk: 15 min, Yamanote to Nippori + 10 min walk

p95.why: Jimbocho is 170 second-hand bookshops on one crossroads, with ukiyo-e print dealers, map shops, vintage magazine stalls and the densest run of curry houses in Tokyo (Bondy, Kyoeido, Ethiopia). You browse the pavement boxes, buy a print or a poster, and eat European-style Japanese curry for lunch.
p95.only: Your 'Ultra cool place. Must go' note is right: nowhere else combines old paper and curry like this. Vintage Jinbocho on your list is one of the shops inside it, so they are the same stop.
p95.vr: A half day that fits Nov 24 between Kappabashi and Akihabara (10 min apart); most shops shut on Sunday, so Tuesday is right.
p95.tk: 10 min, Hanzomon or Mita line to Jimbocho

p96.why: Tsuen has sold tea at the east end of Uji bridge since 1160, which makes it the oldest tea shop in the world, and you sit in the wooden shop over a bowl of matcha and a sweet for about ¥1,000 looking at the river. Uji is the matcha town, 20 minutes from Kyoto.
p96.only: Age is the uniqueness: 860 years in the same family. Ippodo in central Kyoto has better tea to take home; Tsuen is where you drink it in the place it comes from.
p96.vr: It only fits if you spend a half day in Uji (Byodo-in, the Nintendo Museum, Tsuen), which the current plan does not have; a Friday afternoon swap for Arashiyama would do it.
p96.ky: 20 min, JR Nara line to Uji

p97.why: Ichimonjiya Wasuke has grilled aburi-mochi beside Imamiya shrine since the year 1000: thumb-sized rice cakes rolled in kinako, charcoal-grilled on bamboo skewers and drowned in white miso sauce, ¥600 a plate with tea. You sit on the veranda facing the rival shop across the lane that has done the same since 1600.
p97.only: The oldest wagashi shop in Japan and one of the oldest businesses anywhere; the dish exists only on this lane. Nakatanidou in Nara is the pounded-mochi show, this is the quiet original.
p97.vr: Closed Wednesdays, open the rest; it is in north Kyoto near Daitoku-ji, 15 minutes by taxi from Ohara's bus route, so it fits the Sunday if you give it an hour.

p98.why: teamLab's newest museum, opened October 2025 a ten-minute walk from Kyoto station: a dark maze of rooms where sculptures of light respond to your body, including works not shown anywhere else. Ninety minutes, timed entry, and the 09:00 slot is the quiet one.
p98.only: The only teamLab with works unique to it and the one with the shortest queue right now; Planets in Tokyo is the barefoot water one, Borderless the biggest. Prices vary by slot, roughly ¥3,400 to 5,200 for adults.
p98.vr: If you do one teamLab on this trip, this is the fresh one and it is next to the station you arrive at on Friday; book the 09:30 slot for Nov 20 and you walk out at 11:00 into the rest of Kyoto.
p98.ky: 10 min walk from the Hachijo exit

p99.why: Lammtarra is an Akihabara chain of adult video and goods shops, and the Epicali branch is several floors of it in the middle of Electric Town. It is part of the district's furniture rather than a destination, and it is 18+.
p99.only: Nothing you cannot see in any other Akihabara adult shop; Super Potato and Radio Center are the floors in that part of town worth your time.
p99.vr: Your 'DVD store' note suggests you expected a film shop; this is not that, and Jimbocho's poster dealers or Tower Records serve the film and music itch far better.

p100.why: A ten-seat counter near Waseda that opened in June 2026 and serves exactly two things: a Korean-style spicy tegutan ramen and a sweet-sauce bibim cold noodle, ¥1,000 each, cash only, with a chatty owner. The broth is sweet first, then the chilli builds.
p100.only: Your 'Peak Ramen' note and a 4.8 rating from locals, so it is a real find; it is a Korean-Japanese hybrid, not a classic tonkotsu, which makes it different from Ichiran and Fuunji. Fuunji remains the better tsukemen if you only have one ramen slot.
p100.vr: Waseda is 15 minutes from Shinjuku, so it works as the Nov 17 lunch after Nakano or a Nov 24 dinner; bring cash.
p100.tk: 20 min, Tozai line to Waseda + 8 min walk

p101.why: The all-day restaurant on the 31st floor of the Tokyo EDITION Toranomon: a glass box above Tokyo Tower with a wood-fired grill, steaks and a long breakfast. The view is the dish; a steak dinner runs ¥12,000 to 20,000, breakfast about ¥5,000.
p101.only: The best Tokyo Tower view of any table on your list, and a quieter room than the New York Bar; for the steak itself, Akasaka Raimon's yakiniku is the better meat for less money.
p101.vr: A splurge breakfast on Nov 25 before Narita would be the one slot it fits, and even then the Skyliner timing is tight; otherwise it is money the camera budget wants.

p102.why: A thatched tea house on the old Tokaido stone road that has served amazake (sweet, alcohol-free rice drink) and charcoal-grilled chikara-mochi to travellers since the 1600s. You sit on the earthen floor by the hearth for 25 minutes, and it is the same stop Edo-period walkers made.
p102.only: The only surviving Edo-era tea house on the Hakone section of the Tokaido and the same place as my Amazake Chaya suggestion, so rate them as one; nothing else on the trip is this old and still doing its original job.
p102.vr: It is already on the Thursday drive at 12:55, ten minutes from the Turnpike gate, and the amazake plus mochi is ¥1,000 well spent.
p102.tk: 1 h 45 by car via the Tomei and Route 1; 2 h by train and bus

p103.why: Nine floors of physical music in the city that still buys CDs: J-pop and city pop floors, a vinyl floor with Japanese pressings, a bookshop, a cafe and in-store events most evenings. It is the counterpart to Disk Union's used crates, all new stock and gift-wrapped.
p103.only: The largest record store in the world, and the only place to find new Japanese pressings and city-pop reissues in one aisle; for used vinyl, Shimokitazawa and Disk Union are cheaper and deeper.
p103.vr: Thirty minutes on a Shibuya evening, two minutes from the Mandarake; it is open to 22:00 so it can be the last stop of a night.
p103.tk: 15 min, Yamanote to Shibuya + 5 min walk

p104.why: Two lanes of 60 yakitori and motsu stalls squeezed between the Shinjuku tracks and the station, smoke in the air, eight stools per shop, ¥300 to 500 a skewer and a beer. You pick a stall by the smell, eat for 40 minutes, and move on to Golden Gai.
p104.only: The same place as my Omoide Yokocho suggestion and the alley Bar Albatross lives in, so they are one stop; Golden Gai is bars, this is food with the same postwar feel.
p104.vr: First night dinner, five minutes from UNPLAN, nothing to book; it is already Nov 16 at 19:00.
p104.tk: 20 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku + 3 min walk

s01.why: Two lanes of tiny yakitori counters jammed against the Yamanote tracks, lit by lanterns and smoke. You sit shoulder to shoulder with salarymen, order skewers by pointing, and drink a highball in the oldest-looking corner of Shinjuku. This is on your own Drinks list too, so both of us think it belongs on night one.
s01.only: Nothing here is the best yakitori in Tokyo, but no other alley puts this many 8-seat grills in one 50 m strip, 5 minutes from your bed. The reason to come is the room, not the food.
s01.vr: It is next to UNPLAN, needs no booking, and is the cheapest possible first-night culture shock.
s01.tk: 15 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku west exit

s02.why: Six narrow lanes of about 200 bars, most seating six people, each with its own theme and a master who runs the room. You pick one by the sign, pay a cover or not, and talk to whoever is next to you. It is the bar scene films copy, surviving next to a hyper-modern district.
s02.only: No other bar district in Japan has this density of one-owner rooms; Pontocho in Kyoto is prettier but formal, Ura-Namba is rougher. Look for bars that write 'no charge' or 'English OK' on the door, and skip anything with a tout.
s02.vr: Walking distance from your hostel on a jet-lag night, and the one thing you will describe to everyone back home.

s03.why: Tonkotsu ramen eaten alone in a wooden booth with a curtain in front, ordered from a vending machine and a tick-box sheet. The solo-booth theatre is the point; the bowl is consistent rather than great.
s03.only: This is the Ichiran from the memes, open 24 hours. For better tonkotsu in the same area, Ramen Hayashida or Fuunji's tsukemen beat it on taste; Ichiran wins on the experience and on being open at 2 a.m.
s03.vr: Do it once, late at night after Golden Gai, when nothing else is open and the booth gimmick is funniest.

s04.why: A 15-seat counter where you dip thick cold noodles into a chicken-and-fish broth so dense it coats the bowl. Locals queue 30 to 50 minutes; you eat in 12. It is the tsukemen people name when asked for the best in Shinjuku.
s04.only: Fuunji's broth is the reference for the 'chicken + dried fish' style; Ichiran is a different dish altogether. If the queue is over 40 minutes, Hayashida 10 minutes away is a fine no-queue substitute.
s04.vr: Worth the queue once; fits the Shinjuku afternoon on Nov 17 if you arrive at 16:45 before the dinner rush.

s05.why: The main Disk Union building plus separate rock, jazz, punk and Latin annexes within two blocks. Used vinyl graded and priced honestly, thousands of Japanese pressings with the obi strip still on, and a listening station on each floor.
s05.only: Japanese pressings with obi, domestic-only jazz issues and ¥500 bargain bins you will not find on Discogs at that price. Compared with Tower Records this is used and deep, not new and broad; compared with Shimokitazawa it is bigger but less fun to browse.
s05.vr: If vinyl is still on your buy list this is the single best stop, and it is 5 minutes from the hostel.

s06.why: A 24-hour discount tower where you buy Kit Kat flavours, snacks, cosmetics, phone cases and oddities in one basket, with a jingle on loop. Tax-free counter on the way out. It is where the first-night 'Japan has everything' feeling comes from.
s06.only: Same stock as every Donki, but this one is open all night 5 minutes from your hostel, so gift shopping can happen at 1 a.m. instead of eating a daytime slot. Prices are not special; convenience is.
s06.vr: Use it as the gift dump on a late night rather than a destination; skip it if you want to save suitcase space for Kappabashi and Onitsuka.

s07.why: An arcade floor with a bar inside Kabukicho Tower, the 48-storey entertainment block that opened in 2023. You play rhythm and crane games with a drink in hand, then ride down through a food hall styled like a neon back alley.
s07.only: The tower itself is the newest piece of Tokyo cyberpunk: the ground-floor Kabuki-yokocho food court is a built set of a Showa alley with K-pop lighting. Akihabara's GiGO has more and better machines; this has the atmosphere and the bar.
s07.vr: Fun for 45 minutes on night one but the arcades in Akihabara on Nov 23 are the serious version.

s09.why: The 400 m pedestrian street that defined kawaii: crepe stands, Calbee+ fresh chips, purikura photo booths, cheap accessories and teenagers in costume on a Sunday. You walk it in 20 minutes, eat a crepe, take a purikura, and leave.
s09.only: Purikura booths that beautify your face and a crepe menu with 80 options exist elsewhere, but nowhere else is the whole street a single genre. It is a scene to see once, not a place to buy.
s09.vr: A quick 20-minute walk-through on the Nov 24 Harajuku block; crowds on a weekday morning are bearable, on a weekend they are not.

s10.why: Five floors of character goods on Omotesando: Tamagotchi, Sanrio, Snoopy, Studio Ghibli, Miffy, with a Japan-only Snoopy Town in the basement. It is the toy stop for gifts people actually want.
s10.only: Kiddy Land stocks Japan-exclusive Sanrio and Ghibli lines and limited collaborations before they reach the Pokémon Center crowd; prices are retail, not discount. For retro games or figures it is the wrong shop, go to Mandarake or Super Potato instead.
s10.vr: Only if you owe gifts to people who like characters; otherwise 15 minutes of looking.
s10.tk: 25 min, Yamanote to Harajuku + 8 min walk

s11.why: The brand's flagship on Omotesando with the full range: Mexico 66 in colours not exported, the leather NIPPON MADE line, and staff who fit you properly. You try three sizes, pay tax-free, and walk out with the shoe you asked about.
s11.only: Japan-only colourways and the NIPPON MADE line are stocked here in depth; the Mexico 66 costs about ¥15,000 against ₹10,000+ in India for less choice. The Ginza NIPPON MADE store is the specialist, this is the generalist with more sizes.
s11.vr: If Onitsuka is on your buy list, one of the two stores is a must; do this one if you want the normal range, Ginza if you want the embroidered one.

s12.why: A room of mame shiba, the small shiba inu, where you sit on the floor for a timed slot while the dogs ignore you, then nap on you. Thirty minutes, a drink included, and photos allowed.
s12.only: Nowhere else on the list has animals; it is the one slot of pure softness in a trip of neon and roads. The dogs are well kept but it is a business; if that bothers you, Meiji Jingu's forest is next door.
s12.vr: A 30-minute happiness break if the Harajuku block has slack; not worth building a day around.

s13.why: The 6th floor of PARCO holds the official Nintendo store, the Pokémon Center Shibuya, the Capcom Store and a Jump shop, with Mandarake three minutes away. You buy official merchandise you cannot order from India and see the Nintendo exclusives.
s13.only: Nintendo TOKYO sells Japan-only apparel and the special-edition hardware colours; Pokémon Center has region-exclusive plush and cards. For used games and figures Mandarake and Super Potato are cheaper and stranger.
s13.vr: Twenty minutes of official-merch shopping on the Nov 24 Shibuya block; easy to combine with Tower Records next door.

s14.why: Three floors of retro consoles and cartridges, Famicom through PS2, with a tiny arcade corner at the top where you play Street Fighter II for ¥100. Famicom carts from ¥300, boxed Super Famicom sets, Game Boys by the crate.
s14.only: The deepest retro-game stock in Tokyo and the only place to find things like LSD Dream Emulator or Japanese-only Famicom titles on the shelf. Prices are 20 to 40 percent above Mandarake and BookOff, so browse here, buy the common stuff elsewhere.
s14.vr: For someone into retro games this is the single most on-brand shop in Akihabara, 15 minutes well spent even if you buy nothing.

s15.why: A 1,300-year-old shrine on the hill above Akihabara that has become the engineers' shrine: IT companies bring new servers for blessing and the charms are for data safety. Next door, Amanoya has served amazake, the sweet rice drink, since 1846, warm in a dark wooden room.
s15.only: The only shrine in Tokyo selling a circuit-board IT-safety omamori, and the only amazake house on your lists in Tokyo. As a shrine it is small; Senso-ji is grander, Meiji Jingu calmer.
s15.vr: A ten-minute uphill detour from Akihabara that gives you a charm for your laptop and a warm cup; fits Nov 23 between the shops.
s15.tk: 8 min, Chuo line to Ochanomizu + 5 min walk

s16.why: One street of guitar shops stacked on both sides: Ishibashi, Kurosawa, Shimokura, ESP. Used Japanese Fenders and Tokai copies you can play unprompted, pedal walls, strings for a third of the Indian price.
s16.only: Japanese-market guitars (Fender Japan, Tokai, Greco) at used prices unavailable in India, and shops that let you plug in without buying. If you are not carrying a guitar home, strings, picks and small pedals are the realistic haul.
s16.vr: A 20-minute walk-through between Akihabara and Jimbocho if the guitarist in you is awake; skip if the suitcase is full.

s17.why: Two arcades on the same block: HEY for retro shooters and fighting games on original cabinets (Darius, Street Fighter III, Gradius), GiGO for crane games, rhythm games and the new stuff. You spend ¥100 at a time and an hour disappears.
s17.only: HEY is one of the last arcades where the shmup and fighting floors are full of originals and the regulars are serious; nothing in Shinjuku matches it. Mikado in Takadanobaba is the other one on the list, more retro-fighter, less variety.
s17.vr: An hour in HEY is the retro-gaming experience you cannot get at home, and it is next to Super Potato.

s19.why: A small Ginza store stocking only the NIPPON MADE line: leather Mexico 66 and Fabre models made in Japan, including the embroidered editions. Staff fit you and the box comes with the made-in-Japan paperwork.
s19.only: The embroidered NIPPON MADE shoes (¥30,000 to 45,000) are here in all sizes; Omotesando has some, Indian stores have none. If you want the regular Mexico 66 go to Omotesando instead, it has more colours.
s19.vr: Only if the embroidered line is the one you want; otherwise Omotesando covers Onitsuka with less walking.

s20.why: Twelve floors of pens, paper, washi, notebooks and ink, with a pen-testing counter and a vegetable farm on the top floor feeding the cafe. You buy small, flat gifts that survive a suitcase and look expensive.
s20.only: The widest Japanese stationery range under one roof, including Itoya own-brand paper and fountain-pen inks not exported; Tokyu Hands and Loft are broader but shallower. Best gift stop on the trip for weight-to-impression ratio.
s20.vr: Thirty minutes on Nov 23 in Ginza solves most of your gift list; it sits between the antique market and the Sony store.

s21.why: Sony's Ginza block, rebuilt as a part-park part-showroom where you try the newest cameras, headphones, PS5 titles and the odd prototype. Free, no pressure, and the staff know the products.
s21.only: The one place to handle Sony's full camera and audio line before deciding anything; for a Fujifilm buyer it is a useful sanity check, for an engineer it is a design-reference walk. Yodobashi has the same products in a louder room.
s21.vr: Twenty minutes if you are in Ginza on Nov 23 anyway; nothing here is unique to Japan except the prototypes.

s22.why: About 250 stalls of antiques in the courtyard of the Tokyo International Forum: vintage kimono, Showa tin toys, tools, ceramics, old cameras, woodblock prints. You flagged it; it falls on the holiday Monday Nov 23 and runs 09:00 to 16:00 unless it rains.
s22.only: Japan's biggest regular outdoor antique market and the only one on your dates in Tokyo; Toji in Kyoto on the 21st is bigger and rougher, this one is curated and pricier. Old cameras and sword fittings appear here more than anywhere else.
s22.vr: It is the reason the Sunday train back exists, and a holiday Monday edition will be the fullest of the year; be there at 09:00.
s22.tk: 3 min walk from Tokyo Station Marunouchi side

s23.why: The top of the Hakone Turnpike at 1,011 m: a car park, the Skylounge cafe, and Fuji standing over Lake Ashi with Sagami Bay behind you. In an MX-5 the 13.8 km climb to get here is the point; the view is the reward.
s23.only: The only viewpoint on the trip where you arrive by a proper touge road rather than a car park off a highway, and the one with both Fuji and the Pacific in the same turn of the head. Jukkoku has a similar view from a cable car; this one you drive to.
s23.vr: It is the climax of the Thursday drive and the picture you will keep; only skip if the Turnpike is closed for weather.
s23.tk: on the drive day, 1 h 45 by car from Tokyo

s24.why: A ridge toll road above the west shore of Lake Ashi with the Mikuni Pass lookout: Fuji across the water, few cars, 10 km of curves. Toll about ¥630.
s24.only: Closer to the lake than the Turnpike and quieter, but the Fuji view is the same one you get from Daikanzan and Jukkoku. Worth driving only if the Thursday timing opens up.
s24.vr: Off the loop since the Izu night came back; only if Thursday runs early and you want more road.
s24.tk: on the drive day, 2 h by car

s25.why: A short, almost empty toll road on the ridge west of Hakone facing Fuji, between Kojiri and Nagao Pass. Toll about ¥360. Pure driving, no stops.
s25.only: The emptiest tarmac in Hakone and the most Fuji-facing, but it duplicates the Ashinoko Skyline and the Turnpike on scenery.
s25.vr: Extra road for the sake of road; only if you have the time and the fuel.
s25.tk: on the drive day, 2 h by car

s26.why: A free lay-by on Route 138 between Sengokuhara and Gotemba where Fuji fills the windscreen. Stop, photograph, go.
s26.only: Free and on a through-road, but Jukkoku and Daikanzan already cover this view from higher up. It only matters if you leave Hakone toward Gotemba, which the current loop does not.
s26.vr: Not on the loop and redundant with the Thursday viewpoints.
s26.tk: on the drive day, 1 h 45 by car

s27.why: A hillside lookout above Lake Yamanaka with Fuji across the water, 20 minutes from Gotemba. Classic morning light, cold, and empty on a weekday.
s27.only: Fuji over a lake with no town in between, cleaner than Kawaguchiko's view; but it sits east of the loop and the Chureito, Shoji and Motosu stops cover the Fuji-and-water genre.
s27.vr: Not on the Wednesday route; adding it costs 45 minutes you need for Obuchi Sasaba at sunset.
s27.tk: on the drive day, 2 h by car

s28.why: Lakeside park on the north shore of Kawaguchiko with flower beds in front and Fuji across the water. Kochia bushes are brown by late November; the view is still the postcard one. Lake Bake next door is shut on Wednesdays.
s28.only: The most accessible Fuji-over-water view, which is why it is the busiest; Lake Shoji and Motosu on the same day are the same view with a tenth of the people. Only worth it if you are ahead of schedule.
s28.vr: Optional on Nov 18 only if the morning ran early; Motosu is the better version later the same afternoon.
s28.tk: on the drive day, 2 h by car

s29.why: Climb 398 steps to the five-storey Chureito Pagoda and look back at Fuji over Fujiyoshida. It is the single most photographed Japan frame; maples around the pagoda hold colour into late November. Forty minutes round trip.
s29.only: The only Fuji view on the trip with a traditional building in the foreground; everything else is lake, tea field or road. Crowded but not Kyoto-crowded on a Wednesday.
s29.vr: The day's hero shot and on the route; the steps are the only cost.
s29.tk: on the drive day, 1 h 45 by car

s30.why: A roadside station on the Asagiri plateau, Fuji's west side, with open pasture and the mountain filling the whole sky. Free parking, soft-serve from the local dairy, and the Food Park with the tea house next door.
s30.only: The only stop where Fuji appears with nothing in front of it at all, no lake and no town, from the quiet west side. The Fuji-view tea stop at Fujien in the Food Park is the actual reason to pull in.
s30.vr: A natural 20-minute leg-stretch between Motosu and the tea fields; the Food Park tea is the part not to skip.
s30.tk: on the drive day, 2 h 15 by car

s31.why: Backup rental office at Gotemba for the old one-way plan: a compact car collected here and dropped at Atami. Unlimited kilometres, about ¥7,000 to 9,000.
s31.only: Only relevant if the OnlyJDM MX-5 falls through; a Toyota compact is a transport solution, not a drive.
s31.vr: The MX-5 is booked in principle; this stays as a fallback only.

s32.why: Return office of the backup one-way plan at Atami, 25 minutes by JR from Ito. Nothing to do here except hand over keys.

s33.why: The JDM rental garage in Sengokuhara. Self-drive needs 26 and three years of licence, which rules you out; their guided drives (an instructor in the passenger seat, you driving a Swift or an RX-7) have no age rule, from about ¥35,000 for two hours.
s33.only: The only way to drive a genuine 90s JDM sports car on this trip if the MX-5 plan collapses; the guided format is restrictive and the kilometres are capped.
s33.vr: Backup to the OnlyJDM MX-5; worth a call only if that booking fails.

s34.why: A 1928 three-storey wooden ryokan on the Ito river, kept as a museum: creaking corridors, carved transoms, a top-floor room with the bay in the window, and a public bath you can book. ¥500, three minutes from K's House.
s34.only: The best-preserved Showa-era wooden inn open to the public on the whole route, and the one piece of 'old Japan' on the car days. Tokyo's Sawanoya is a working ryokan, not a museum; this is the architecture itself.
s34.vr: Thirty minutes before you leave Ito on Nov 19; it opens at 09:00 and you are next door.

s35.why: On the 21st of every month about a thousand stalls fill Toji temple's grounds: old kimono by the kilo, tools, ceramics, tansu chests, prints, knives, plus street food. It opens at dawn and the good stuff is gone by nine. This is the garage-sale Kyoto you asked for.
s35.only: Bigger and rougher than the Oedo market, with real bargains (kimono ¥500 to 2,000, old tools, sword fittings) and no English, which is the charm. The pagoda behind it is Japan's tallest wooden one.
