s35.vr: It falls exactly on your Kyoto Saturday and only happens once a month; be there at 07:00 before the car.

s36.why: The ramen district of Kyoto, a kilometre of shops on Higashioji-dori in Ichijoji: Gokkei's thick chicken broth, Takayasu's karaage, and the original Tenkaippin. Ten minutes from Enkōji, so it is the Sunday lunch.
s36.only: Kyoto's own ramen style, kotteri (thick) chicken, is only done properly here; Kyoto Station's Ramen Koji is a sampler of other regions. Gokkei is the one to queue for, Takayasu is faster.
s36.vr: The natural lunch after Enkōji on Nov 22, and the only Kyoto-style ramen on the trip.
s36.ky: 25 min, bus 5 or Eizan line to Ichijoji

s37.why: A 17th-century poet's hermitage with a small garden of clipped azaleas, white sand and maples, where you sit on the veranda and hear the bamboo deer-scarer knock. ¥700, five minutes on foot from Enkōji, a quarter of the visitors.
s37.only: The calmest garden on the list: Enkōji is the famous one next door with the reservation system, Shisen-do is where you actually sit still for 20 minutes. Late-November colour here is usually at its best.
s37.vr: Pair it with Enkōji on Nov 22; it is the quiet half of the morning.

s38.why: The main Zen temple of Arashiyama with the Sogenchi pond garden, which uses the mountain behind as borrowed scenery. ¥500 for the garden. The bamboo grove starts at its north gate, so you do the garden first and exit into the grove.
s38.only: The one Arashiyama ticket that is worth paying for; the grove itself is free and 10 minutes. On a holiday weekend this is the busiest temple in Kyoto, so your Friday-morning slot matters.
s38.vr: Worth it only as the way into the grove before 10:00 on the Friday; after that, Kurama or the far west end of Arashiyama is the better morning.
s38.ky: 20 min, JR Sagano line to Saga-Arashiyama

s39.why: After dark Kodai-ji lights its maple-ringed pond and the bamboo path, with a projection show on the raked gravel. It is the best night garden you can walk to from Gion, 20 minutes from your hostel.
s39.only: Night illuminations exist only in autumn and spring and only in Kyoto at this scale; Eikando is bigger, Kodai-ji is closer and finishes in an hour. Colour will be early-peak on Nov 20 this year.
s39.vr: Fits Friday night after GEAR if you have energy; Eikando on Saturday is the stronger version if you only do one.

s40.why: Eikando's autumn illumination is the famous one: 3,000 maples lit around a pond, a hillside pagoda, and the Amida statue that looks over its shoulder. ¥700 after dark, roughly Nov 7 to Dec 6, verify the dates.
s40.only: The most-photographed maple light-up in Japan, which also makes it the most crowded; the holiday weekend will be shoulder to shoulder. If you want lit maples with space, Kodai-ji or Shisen-do by day are the alternatives.
s40.vr: Spectacular but you return from the Nara mountains on Saturday evening; only if the drive is back by 18:30 and you can face a queue.

s41.why: A 500 m lantern-lit lane between the Kamo river and Kawaramachi, lined with bars, izakaya and the odd tea house, geisha occasionally crossing. You walk it after GEAR, pick a bar with a river-side window, and that is the Kyoto night.
s41.only: Prettier than Golden Gai and more formal; the river-facing rooms are the point. Some doors are members-only, so choose places with a menu outside.
s41.vr: It is 5 minutes from Len and after GEAR you want exactly one drink in a lane like this.
s41.ky: 15 min, bus or Karasuma line to Shijo

s42.why: A 400 m covered food street: pickles, tofu doughnuts, dashi shops, matcha sweets and Aritsugu, the 1560 knife maker. You taste your way down and buy the knife or the tea tools here if Kappabashi is not enough.
s42.only: Aritsugu is the one knife shop on the trip with a 460-year history, and the pickle and dashi stalls are Kyoto-only. It is tourist-heavy now; for eating go to Ichijoji, for buying come here.
s42.vr: Thirty minutes between Tozando and Ippodo on the Friday afternoon; a chance to compare Aritsugu to Seisuke before you buy.

s43.why: The main store of a tea house founded in 1717: matcha, gyokuro and sencha in tins, chasen whisks, and a tea room upstairs where staff teach you to whisk a bowl. You buy tea here, not at the airport.
s43.only: Ippodo's Ummon and Sayaka matcha are the grades Kyoto tea ceremony uses and cost half of what they do abroad; Tsuen in Uji on your list is older but a cafe, this is the shop. Also sells the tea you drank in the fields on Nov 18, from a different grower.
s43.vr: The most reliable tea purchase on the trip, 10 minutes from Len, and the tea room is the calm half-hour your Friday needs.

s44.why: The mochi shop in Nara where staff pound rice at full speed with a wooden mallet every half hour, then sell the warm yomogi mochi for ¥200. You watch, eat one on the kerb, and that is the Nara snack.
s44.only: Mochi warm from the mallet is the thing; Ichimonjiya Wasuke in Kyoto on your list is the older and more atmospheric sweet, this is the louder one. Both in one trip is fine, they are different sweets.
s44.vr: Five minutes on the way through Nara on Nov 21, and it is ¥200.

s45.why: A shrine in the deer forest with 3,000 bronze and stone lanterns along the paths and inside the halls, 20 minutes on foot from Todai-ji. The inner garden costs ¥500; the lantern-lined approach is free.
s45.only: The lantern forest exists nowhere else; Todai-ji is the giant Buddha, this is the atmosphere. Late afternoon with low light through the cedars is when it works.
s45.vr: Only if the Nara stop on Nov 21 has 45 minutes spare after Todai-ji; it is the better of the two for photographs.

s46.why: Osaka's 1912 'new world', built around the Tsutenkaku tower and now a Showa-era neon district of kushikatsu bars, pachinko and old men's cafes. Deep-fried skewers, no double dipping, a beer, and the tower lit at night.
s46.only: The most retro-neon street in Japan, more Blade Runner than Shinjuku because nothing has been renovated. It needs an Osaka night, which the current plan no longer has.
s46.vr: Osaka is dropped; this comes back only if you choose an Osaka evening over the Sunday-night return.
s46.tk: 3 h, Nozomi to Shin-Osaka + Midosuji line

s47.why: The neon canal: the Glico runner, the giant crab, takoyaki stands, crowds on the Ebisu bridge. You walk it once at night, eat takoyaki standing up, and photograph the reflections.
s47.only: The single most cyberpunk frame in Kansai, but it is 20 minutes of walking in a crowd; everything else in Osaka is better than Dotonbori itself.
s47.vr: Only if Osaka returns to the plan; it costs the Sunday-evening train.
s47.tk: 3 h, Nozomi to Shin-Osaka + Midosuji line

s48.why: The back streets of Namba: standing bars, tiny izakaya, and the Misono Building, a 1950s block whose second floor is a corridor of 40 bars with six seats each. Osaka's Golden Gai, with cheaper drinks and louder people.
s48.only: Friendlier and cheaper than Golden Gai, and nobody charges a cover; it is the best bar night in Japan for a solo traveller, which is why it hurts that Osaka is gone.
s48.vr: Only if an Osaka night comes back; then this, not Dotonbori, is the reason.
s48.tk: 3 h, Nozomi to Shin-Osaka + Midosuji line

s49.why: Osaka's electronics and otaku district: retro-game shops, figure stores, parts shops, maid cafes, smaller and cheaper than Akihabara.
s49.only: Retro game prices run 10 to 20 percent under Akihabara, but the stock is shallower; if you do Akihabara on Nov 23 there is no reason to repeat it here.
s49.vr: Redundant with Akihabara and Osaka is off the plan.
s49.tk: 3 h, Nozomi to Shin-Osaka + Midosuji line

s50.why: Nintendo's own museum in its old Uji factory: every console and controller ever made on one floor, giant-controller games you play with a partner, and a hanafuda workshop. Tickets are a lottery drawn three months ahead.
s50.only: The only Nintendo museum in the world, 30 minutes from Kyoto. Without a ticket it is a locked door; the November lottery closed in August, so only a last-minute release on the site could get you in.
s50.vr: Check the ticket site once in the week before; if a slot appears on Nov 20 or 22 it jumps to must, otherwise it is impossible.
s50.ky: 30 min, JR Nara line to Ogura

s51.why: A hostel in a converted toy warehouse in Kuramae with a wooden bar-lounge on the ground floor, dorms upstairs, 10 minutes to Asakusa on foot and 25 to the Skyliner at Ueno. Your base for the last three nights.
s51.only: The lounge is where solo travellers meet people in Tokyo; the location puts Kappabashi, Asakusa, the Sumida river and the Nov 25 airport train within half an hour. Not booked yet.
s51.vr: The right base for the shopping days; book it before dorms fill for the holiday weekend.

s52.why: Your booked hostel for the first two nights: mixed dorm, breakfast, a bar-lounge that runs events, 10 minutes to Golden Gai and 5 to the Chuo line for the camera trip to Nakano.
s52.only: Booked and paid, ¥16,100 for both nights, non-refundable. Check-in 16:00 to 23:00.

s53.why: A hostel with a cafe-bar on Kawaramachi, walking distance to Pontocho, GEAR and Nishiki, 15 minutes to Kyoto Station for the Saturday car. Two nights, Nov 20 and 21.
s53.only: Central enough to skip buses at night, which in Kyoto on a holiday weekend saves an hour a day. Not booked yet, and Kyoto dorms sell out for Nov 21 to 23.
s53.vr: Book now; the three-day weekend is the worst of the year for Kyoto beds.

s54.why: A Namba hostel with a record shop in the lobby, 10 minutes from Dotonbori. Only relevant if an Osaka night returns.
s54.only: The record shop is the gimmick; otherwise a standard dorm.

s55.why: teamLab's borderless museum in Azabudai Hills: rooms of projected light that flow into each other, a crystal corridor, a tea house where flowers bloom in your cup. Timed tickets ¥3,800 to 4,800, two hours.
s55.only: Borderless is the one without a path; Planets in Toyosu, which is on your list, is the one where you walk barefoot through water. If you do one, Planets is more physical and more Instagram, Borderless is more cerebral. teamLab Biovortex in Kyoto is the newest and least crowded of the three.
s55.vr: Only if you want a second teamLab after Planets or Biovortex; one is enough for most people.

s56.why: The shopping maze under Tokyo Station: Character Street (Pokémon, Jump, Ghibli, NHK), Tokyo Banana and Kit Kat boutiques, and Ramen Street. You clear the edible-gift list in 30 minutes on the way off the Shinkansen.
s56.only: Tokyo Banana and the limited Kit Kat flavours are sold here before anywhere else, and the station is where you arrive on Nov 22 anyway. Not a place to linger.
s56.vr: Thirty minutes on arrival from Kyoto and the gift box is solved.

s57.why: A street of 90 fabric shops by Nippori station, Tomato being the five-floor anchor: Japanese cotton, noren curtains, tenugui towels, kimono remnants at ¥100 a metre. Gifts for people who sew, or a noren for your own door.
s57.only: Noren and tenugui here cost a third of what tourist shops in Asakusa charge, and the kimono remnants are by the metre. Some shops shut on Sundays.
s57.vr: Only if someone at home sews or you want a noren; otherwise Asakusa covers textiles with less travel.

s58.why: A 1908 knife and kitchen shop on Kappabashi with 80 knife types laid out by use, engraving on the spot, and staff who explain steel in English. Also pans, kettles and tea pots. Second opinion before you buy at Seisuke.
s58.only: Kama-Asa stocks Japanese carbon-steel brands at maker prices and engraves your name in kanji free; Seisuke up the road is bigger on stainless and faster. Comparing the two takes 20 minutes and is worth it on a ¥20,000 knife.
s58.vr: If a knife is on your list, do Seisuke and Kama-Asa back to back on Nov 24 and buy at the one that felt right.

s59.why: A shrine inside a 70-hectare planted forest next to Harajuku station: a gravel avenue under the torii, the sake-barrel wall, a wedding on most weekend mornings. Free, open sunrise to sunset.
s59.only: The one large forest in central Tokyo, planted a century ago and now self-sustaining; Shinjuku Gyoen is a garden, this is woods. Ginkgo at the entrance turns late November.
s59.vr: Twenty quiet minutes before Harajuku's noise on Nov 24; start here, not after.

s60.why: The fast train to Narita: 36 to 41 minutes from Nippori or Ueno to Terminal 2, ¥2,580, reserved seats. Book the 07:20 or so for an 11:10 flight.
s60.only: Faster than the Narita Express from your side of town and cheaper; the only alternative from Kuramae is the Access Express, slower but no change.
s60.vr: It is how you get to the flight; reserve the seat the day before.

s62.why: Eight ramen shops from eight regions (Sapporo miso, Hakata tonkotsu, Tokushima, Kyoto's own Masutani) on the 10th floor of Kyoto Station, each with a ticket machine. You eat in 25 minutes and are back on the platform or the bus. It exists for exactly the gap between a train and the next thing.
s62.only: Nothing here is the best version of its style, but it is the only place you can compare four regional ramens in one corridor. For a proper Kyoto bowl, Ichijoji ramen street (s36) or Menya Inoichi near Shijo beats it clearly.
s62.vr: Useful as a fallback lunch on Nov 20 or 22 when you are passing the station, not a destination.
s62.tk: 2 h 15, Nozomi, then 2 min inside the station
s62.ky: 0 min, inside the station, 10F of the Isetan building

s63.why: The outer market survived the fish auction's move to Toyosu, and it is still the breakfast street: tamagoyaki on a stick, grilled scallops with butter, tuna bowls, strawberry daifuku. Go at 07:00, graze stall to stall, finish with coffee at Turret. By 10:30 it is tour-group dense.
s63.only: Kitsuneya (p50) from your list is on the main lane, so this is where that stop lives. The fish itself is fresher and cheaper at Toyosu's Senkyaku Banrai, but that is a shopping-mall version of the mood; the outer market is the real street.
s63.vr: Easy 20-minute hop from Kuramae on the Oedo line, perfect for a Nov 24 breakfast before Kappabashi, as long as you are there before 08:30.

s64.why: The Odakyu Romancecar terminus in Hakone: 85 minutes from Shinjuku in a reserved seat, then buses and the Tozan railway fan out from here. It only matters if the car plan collapses.
s64.only: The practical point: book the Romancecar on the Odakyu site the day before, choose the front observation car on the GSE if you can; the Hakone Freepass covers everything beyond here.
s64.vr: Irrelevant while the MX-5 is booked; it is the fallback route only.
s64.tk: 1 h 25, Romancecar from Shinjuku (Tokyo Station adds 15 min)
s64.ky: 2 h 40, Shinkansen to Odawara + Tozan line

s65.why: The café at the top of the Hakone Turnpike is where the Japanese car scene parks: weekday mornings the lot fills with Roadsters, RX-7s, Skylines and Porsches, and people walk over to talk about your car. Coffee with Fuji and Sagami Bay in the window, then the drive back down.
s65.only: The one place on the trip where the MX-5 is a conversation starter rather than transport. Daikanzan (s23) is the viewpoint; this is the people.
s65.vr: You are driving a Roadster up the Turnpike on Nov 19 anyway; 25 minutes here is the car-culture moment of the whole trip.
s65.tk: on the drive day, 1 h 30 by car via Odawara

s66.why: Same place as Shinjuku Gyoen on your list: 58 hectares of French, English and Japanese gardens ten minutes from UNPLAN, with the Shinjuku towers over the trees. Listed again only as the Nov 17 alternative to the Shimokitazawa afternoon.
s66.only: Of the Tokyo gardens this is the one with real scale and the ginkgo-plus-skyscraper photo; Kiyosumi (p23) is smaller and more refined, Meiji Jingu (s59) is forest rather than garden.
s66.vr: Rate it under p06; this entry only exists so the Day 2 swap works.

s67.why: Under the Ueno tracks, standing bars where office workers drink highballs and eat motsu-ni (simmered offal) and pickled cucumber from 10 in the morning. No seats, no menu in English, ¥300 drinks, and the man beside you will talk to you after the second one. Fifteen minutes and you have seen the real after-work Tokyo.
s67.only: Tachinomi are cheaper and more social than Golden Gai (s02) and nobody is performing for tourists. Takioka is the classic; Daitoryo next door is louder.
s67.vr: Nov 22 evening straight off the Nozomi, Ueno is one stop from Kuramae's area: the right landing drink before the Monday markets.

s69.why: Omoren's Ariake branch, the fun-car rental chain. Their Roadster is already taken for Nov 19, so what remains is a GR86 six-speed manual at ¥43,200 for the two days plus insurance. It is the fallback if OnlyJDM falls through.
s69.only: The practical point: 600 km per 24 h allowance beats OnlyJDM's 200 km, so if you end up here the loop has no distance surcharge.
s69.vr: Fallback only; the OnlyJDM MX-5 is decided and only a cancellation brings this back.

s70.why: Omoren's Shibuya branch with an ND Roadster, closest shop to the Tomei. It was not free for your dates when checked on Nov 7.
s70.only: The practical point: 15 minutes from the Tomei at Tokyo IC, which would have saved an hour of city driving versus Adachi.
s70.vr: Not available for Nov 18–19; keep it only to re-check if your dates move.

s71.why: Omoren Hanzomon: Roadster RF hardtop automatic, GR Supra and GR Yaris, with the longest opening hours of the chain. Only 300 km per 24 h, which the Fuji–Izu loop exceeds.
s71.only: The practical point: an automatic RF if the manual is a worry, but the 300 km cap adds about ¥10,000 of overage on your loop.
s71.vr: Worse value than the OnlyJDM MX-5 for your route; fallback only.

s72.why: Omoren Fuchu's Abarth 124 Spider: the MX-5's Italian twin with a turbo and an automatic, parked beside the Chuo Expressway on the way to Fuji. Cheapest of the fun options at ¥17,870 a day.
s72.only: The practical point: if you cannot get the manual-licence proof together, this is the open-top automatic that still does the Fuji roads with a soundtrack.
s72.vr: Only if the manual licence check fails; otherwise the MX-5 wins on feel.

s73.why: A design hostel in a Nihonbashi back street with a basement bar, a coffee stand and free laundry, 18 minutes from Tokyo Station by the Sobu rapid. The Nov 19 night exists for one thing: the 07:00 Nozomi.
s73.only: The practical point: do the laundry here on night four, pack the day bag for Kyoto, and set two alarms; free cancellation until Nov 18 so it costs nothing to hold.
s73.vr: Not booked yet; it is the right bed for a 06:30 walk to the Shinkansen and worth locking in now.
s73.tk: 8 min by taxi, 18 min by Sobu rapid from Bakurocho

s74.why: A Ginza studio that teaches batto, the art of drawing and cutting: hakama, watch the teacher cut, practise with a mock sword, then a real-blade cut if you wish and the teacher agrees on the day. 45 minutes, ¥18,700. Since August 2025 it runs once a day, at 19:00 on Tue, Thu, Sat and Sun.
s74.only: Unlike the Tozando shop (p65) where you look at swords, here you cut with one; and unlike a Kyoto samurai show, it is a lesson, not a performance. Book a week ahead, slots fill on holidays.
s74.vr: Your sword session is now Waraku in Kyoto (s121). Keep this only if you still want a live blade: Tue Nov 24 at 19:00, after Skytree.

s75.why: The barefoot teamLab: you wade knee-deep through warm water with koi projected around your legs, lie under a hanging garden of orchids, and lose the floor in a mirrored room. 90 minutes, timed tickets, book online.
s75.only: Planets is bodily and wet where Borderless (s55) is a maze of rooms; your list has Planets (p84) so this is the same place. If you only do one teamLab in Tokyo, Planets photographs better and is less of a crowd-herd.
s75.vr: It is on your list; as a Nov 19 evening after the car return it works, but the new Biovortex in Kyoto (p98) may be the fresher pick if you only want one.

s76.why: Six floors of headphones and in-ear monitors on demo, plugged into your own phone, with a used floor where last year's flagships go for half. Staff know the sound signatures and leave you alone otherwise.
s76.only: Japan-only IEM brands (final, Acoustune, Intime) and the used floor are the things you cannot get in Bengaluru; the new-stock prices are only slightly better than online after tax-free.
s76.vr: Worth 40 minutes on the Nov 23 Akihabara pass if audio is on your buy list, otherwise skip.

s77.why: An hour at the Kama-Asa workbench learning to hold the angle and keep the burr on a whetstone, then you sharpen the knife you just bought. Reserve online; English taught.
s77.only: It turns the Kappabashi knife from a souvenir into a tool you can maintain; nobody in Bengaluru will teach you this on a Japanese stone. Pair it with the knife purchase at Kama-Asa (s58) or Seisuke (p70).
s77.vr: If you buy a gyuto on Nov 24 this is the natural next hour; if you don't, skip.

s78.why: The Kabukicho multiplex with the Godzilla head on the roof: 12 screens, IMAX and Dolby Atmos, late shows after 21:00. Watching an anime in Japanese with no subtitles in a packed Shinjuku room is a stranger experience than it sounds.
s78.only: The only cinema on a plaza where Godzilla roars on the hour; check eiga.com for the week's slate, and note Japanese releases are rarely subtitled in English.
s78.vr: A jet-lag-friendly option for Nov 16 if Golden Gai feels like too much; otherwise the Ikebukuro IMAX (s92) is the better screen.

s79.why: Search Meetup for a Tokyo tech, startup or AI event on Nov 23 or 24; most are English-speaking, in Shibuya or Roppongi, and end at a bar. Two hours of talking to engineers who moved to Japan tells you more about working here than any guide.
s79.only: The networking slot; which event depends on that week's listings, so the plan is a search, not a place.
s79.vr: Only if a listing that week looks good; it competes with your last two Tokyo evenings.

s80.why: The Shimokitazawa thrift anchor in a converted bathhouse: racks sorted by colour, a section sold by weight, Japanese and American vintage from the 80s and 90s at prices that still make sense. Bring cash, try things on, they buy clothes too.
s80.only: Same shop as New York Joe on your list (p86); the by-weight corner and the buyback counter are the things you will not find at Nakano or BOOKOFF. For sheer volume, 2nd STREET across the station is bigger but duller.
s80.vr: On your list already; a solid 45 minutes inside the Nov 17 Shimokitazawa afternoon.
s80.tk: 25 min, Odakyu or Inokashira line from Shinjuku/Shibuya

s81.why: Two hours in a Shinjuku kitchen kneading and cutting noodles, building a tare and a broth, then eating your own bowl. Classes run through Cookly or airKitchen with English hosts.
s81.only: Ramen is on your list five times; this is the only entry where you learn why a bowl tastes the way it does. Kyoto's Ramen Factory is the Kansai twin if the Tokyo slots are gone.
s81.vr: Fun but it costs an afternoon of your last Tokyo days, which the shopping list also wants; book only if Nov 24 has air.

s82.why: Takadanobaba's Mikado is the fighting-game arcade that never died: 100-yen cabinets of Street Fighter, Guilty Gear and Samurai Shodown, tournaments streamed nightly, regulars who will beat you and then show you the combo. Open till midnight, two stops from Shinjuku.
s82.only: Unlike GiGO or namco TOKYO (s07, s17) which are claw machines and rhythm games, this is competitive play on original hardware; it is the arcade for someone who grew up on retro games.
s82.vr: Best Tokyo night-two option for you: ¥1,000 goes a long way and it is honest, un-touristed Tokyo.

s83.why: Mend a cracked bowl with lacquer and gold dust in a small Asakusa or Kuramae studio, 90 minutes, and carry it home. The quick-set version uses modern resin; the real urushi takes weeks, so ask which you are getting.
s83.only: Of the craft classes on the list this is the one whose result lasts and means something; the wagashi class (s88) is eaten and the latte class (s90) is a skill, not an object.
s83.vr: Lovely but it competes with the Nov 24 shopping sweep; pick it if you want one quiet hour that day.

s84.why: Hiroyasu Kayama's Benfiddich in Nishi-Shinjuku has no menu: he asks what you like, pulls herbs from jars and absinthe he distilled himself, and makes a drink with a mortar and pestle in front of you. Dark room, eight seats, ¥2,500 a drink.
s84.only: The most awarded bar in Japan for a reason; the Park Hyatt's New York Bar (p77) gives you the view, this gives you the craft. Not for a group, not for a rush, often a queue after 20:00.
s84.vr: One drink here after the Park Hyatt on Nov 17 is the best cocktail hour of the trip, if you are willing to wait at the door.
s84.tk: 15 min, Chuo line to Shinjuku + 8 min walk

s85.why: Tori-no-Ichi is the November rake fair: hundreds of stalls at Otori Shrine sell decorated kumade rakes that scoop in luck for the next year, and every sale ends in a round of rhythmic hand clapping. Food stalls, lanterns, crowds of locals; it runs 24 hours on the day of the rooster.
s85.only: Nov 19 is the second rooster day of 2026, so it only exists on that one night of your trip; no other festival on the list is this date-bound.
s85.vr: If the car is back by 18:30 you can be at Otori Shrine by 20:00; it is the one night-festival chance on the trip and it is 20 minutes from CITAN.

s86.why: A neighbourhood sento five minutes from Nui: ¥550, a hot bath, a cold plunge, a sauna for a few hundred more, and old men who have been coming for forty years. Bring a towel or rent one.
s86.only: Onsen is natural hot-spring water; a sento is city water and city people. After K's House and Tenzan this is the third kind of bath, and the cheapest, most local one.
s86.vr: A 40-minute wind-down any Kuramae night; no need to plan it, just go when your feet hurt.

s87.why: Coffee served like sushi omakase: a counter, a barista who pours five or six cups in sequence, from a fermented Ethiopian to a Japanese-grown bean, explaining each. About 90 minutes, ¥5,000–8,000, booked on their site, next to Kiyosumi Gardens.
s87.only: The most serious coffee experience in Japan; Blue Bottle and the Kiyosumi roasters do a good cup, but nobody else does a course. If you just want the neighbourhood's coffee, Arise or Allpress nearby are ¥600.
s87.vr: Pairs with Kiyosumi Gardens on Nov 24 if you want one slow luxury; expensive for what is, in the end, coffee.

s88.why: Kanshundo's master shows you how to shape nerikiri, the soft bean-paste sweets that look like maples and chrysanthemums; you make four, eat one with matcha and box the rest. 75 minutes, near Yasaka Shrine.
s88.only: Kyoto is the home of wagashi; Marushin in Saitama (s99) sells them, Kanshundo teaches them. It is the easiest craft class to fit into a Kyoto morning.
s88.vr: Nov 21 morning is already Toji market plus the car day, so it only fits if the Nara drive is dropped.

s89.why: Yushakobo is the custom mechanical keyboard shop: kits, switches by the piece, keycap sets, and a bench with soldering irons where you can build on the spot. Staff speak keyboard, and some English.
s89.only: Japanese group-buy keycaps and kits that never ship abroad, and the bench to build before you fly; Yodobashi (p76) sells finished boards, nothing custom. A keyboard is on your buy list, so this is where it is specified.
s89.vr: Forty minutes on the Nov 23 Akihabara pass; buy the kit here, build it at Nui that night.

s90.why: An hour of steaming milk and pouring hearts and rosettas at a Shibuya cafe school; you leave able to do a passable tulip. About ¥5,000, booked ahead.
s90.only: The least Japan-specific class on the list; Bengaluru has latte art courses too. The coffee omakase (s87) is the uniquely Japanese coffee experience.
s90.vr: Nothing about it needs Tokyo; spend the hour on Kappabashi or the sento instead.

s91.why: A hundred solo travellers, four Roppongi bars, free shots, Friday and Saturday only. It is the easiest way to end a night with a table of strangers.
s91.only: Your Tokyo nights are Mon, Tue, Thu, Sun, Mon and Tue, so it does not run while you are there; the Golden Gai hop (s02) and Nui's bar are the solo-traveller substitutes.
s91.vr: Dates do not line up; it runs on weekends and you are in Kyoto both weekend nights.

s92.why: Grand Cinema Sunshine's IMAX Laser GT is a four-storey screen, the biggest in Japan, with 12-channel sound; Shin-Bungeiza next door runs all-night double bills of old anime and yakuza films for ¥1,500. Ikebukuro is also the women-led anime district, Otome Road, if that interests you.
s92.only: The screen is the point: nothing in India or in Shinjuku matches the GT format. Check if a Japanese film you can follow without subtitles is playing in GT that week.
s92.vr: Nov 24 evening if there is a big release in IMAX GT; otherwise the sento and a last Kuramae night are better.

s93.why: Toyota Rent a Car three minutes from the Hachijo exit of Kyoto Station: a Yaris-class compact, about ¥9,600 a day, unlimited km. This is the car for the Nov 21 Mitarai Valley, Dorogawa and Nara loop.
s93.only: The practical point: they need the physical Indian licence, the 1949 IDP and passport; book online a week ahead so a car is actually held, and return before 20:00.
s93.vr: Necessary for the Saturday mountain day; without it the Nara mountains do not happen.
s93.ky: 3 min walk from the Hachijo exit

s94.why: Forty thatched farmhouses in a river valley 90 minutes north of Kyoto, still lived in, with a small folk museum, a soba lunch and a walk up to the shrine behind the village. The hills around are cedar and late maples.
s94.only: The one rural-village landscape on the list that is not a temple town: Shirakawa-go without the buses, Ohara (s97) without the gardens. Needs a car, and in late November it is cold and possibly misty, which suits it.
s94.vr: Only fits if the Nov 21 car goes north instead of south to the Nara mountains; the Mitarai–Dorogawa loop is your own list, so this stays the alternative.
s94.ky: 1 h 30 by car, 2 h by bus

s95.why: Take the little Eizan train 30 minutes north to Kurama, climb through the temple's cedar-root paths over the ridge, and come down to Kibune's river-side shrine and its lantern steps. Two hours of walking, no car, and in late November the maples along the Kibune valley are at peak.
s95.only: The only serious walk on the Kyoto list that starts from a train station, and the only one that replaces Arashiyama's crowds with forest. Shisen-do (s37) is a sit-down version of the same mood.
s95.vr: This is the quieter Friday Nov 20: Arashiyama's bamboo grove on the first morning of a three-day weekend is a queue, Kurama is not.
s95.ky: 50 min, Karasuma line to Kokusaikaikan then bus, or Keihan + Eizan

s96.why: A lakeside onsen hotel at Kawaguchiko with Fuji from the bath: Konansou and Fuji Lake Hotel are the mid-range, Ubuya the splurge. It was the alternative to the Hakone ryokan night before the plan moved to Ito.
s96.only: The practical point: the Nov 18 night is now K's House Ito, which costs a tenth as much; this only comes back if you want the Fuji-from-the-bath photo and are willing to shorten the Izu day.
s96.vr: Superseded by the booked Ito night; keep as a note in case the loop is re-cut.
s96.tk: 1 h 30 by car on the Chuo Expressway, 2 h by Fuji Excursion train

s97.why: A farming valley 40 minutes north of Kyoto by bus. Sanzen-in has the moss garden with the small stone jizo peeking out and a cedar-shaded approach; Hosen-in across the lane frames its 700-year-old pine in a window and serves matcha with the ticket. Walk the lane between them past pickle shops.
s97.only: The gentlest of the famous Kyoto places: the crowd thins the moment you leave the bus, and Ohara's maples turn earlier than the city's, so Nov 22 is close to peak. Enkōji (p08) is smaller and needs a reservation; Ohara does not.
s97.vr: Already your Sunday morning and the best answer to the crowd worry; it is the Kyoto you came for.
s97.ky: 1 h, bus 17 from the station or 45 min from Demachiyanagi

s98.why: A wooden inn street in the mountains south of Nara, 15 minutes from the Mitarai Valley car park: pilgrims' lodges, a public bath (Dorogawa Onsen Center, ¥700) and a river that runs through town. In late November most lodges are quiet and the bath is nearly yours.
s98.only: Onsen in true mountain country rather than a resort; nothing else on the list combines a gorge walk and a hot bath in the same hour. It is the deepest-nature stop of the whole trip.
s98.vr: Your own Mitarai Valley pick is next door, so the bath is the natural end to the gorge walk on Nov 21 before the drive to Nara.
s98.ky: 2 h 15 by car via the Keinawa and Route 309

s99.why: The 85-year-old wagashi master from the video you saved runs this shop in Yoshikawa, Saitama: mitarashi dango grilled fresh, dorayaki, seasonal sweets, open from nine. Fifty minutes out on the Musashino line, in a town with nothing else for a tourist.
s99.only: The dango is honest and the man is the reason to go; for the same craft without the two-hour round trip, Kyoto has Ichimonjiya Wasuke (p97) and Tokyo has a dozen good wagashi counters. Better options exist; this one is personal.
s99.vr: Only worth it if meeting him matters to you; as food alone it costs more time than it gives.

s68.why: Fujiyoshida's own udon: thick, chewy, almost stubborn noodles in a soy-miso broth with cabbage and a slice of horse meat, ¥600, served in what are often people's front rooms, lunch only. Half the shops close by 14:00.
s68.only: Found nowhere else in Japan in this form; it is the lunch that belongs to the retro street (p66) and nothing in Tokyo copies it. Fujinomiya yakisoba (s103) is the other local B-grade dish on the same day.
s68.vr: Lunch on the Nov 18 drive is already here; 25 minutes, cash, and you have eaten the region.
s68.tk: on the drive day, 1 h 45 by car

s100.why: The deepest and quietest of the Fuji Five Lakes, with the view that is on the ¥1,000 note from its north-west shore. Ten minutes out of the car, no shops, no cruise boats.
s100.only: Kawaguchiko (s28) is the busy, built-up lake; Shōji (p81) on your list is the tiny one next door; Motosu is the empty, blue, deep one. Late November gives the clearest Fuji of the year here, in the afternoon light.
s100.vr: Already a ten-minute stop on the Nov 18 drive between Shōji and the tea stops; costs nothing to keep.
s100.tk: on the drive day, 2 h 15 by car

s101.why: Six small producers in the woods beside the Asagiri roadside station: Fujien brews Shizuoka tea with Fuji spring water in a room facing the mountain, Fuji Masa distils sake next door, and the dairy sells the soft serve the whole plateau drives for. Thirty minutes, with the people who make the things.
s101.only: Tea tasting with the grower rather than a tea-shop counter; your tea-with-locals wish fits here better than Ippodo (s43) in Kyoto, which is a shop. The Obuchi Sasaba fields (s102) are where the leaves grow, this is where they are brewed.
s101.vr: Nov 18 at 15:35 as planned; closed Thursdays, so it only works on the Wednesday drive.
s101.tk: on the drive day, 2 h 30 by car

s102.why: Rows of tea bushes running straight at Fuji, kept by farmers on private land outside Fuji city; you stand in the marked viewing lane and the mountain fills the frame behind the green stripes. Free, with a 25-car lot 300 metres away, and the bushes are in small white flower in November.
s102.only: The most Japanese single photograph on the trip and the only tea-field-plus-Fuji view that is open to visitors; Chureito (s29) is the pagoda version of the same idea with a hundred times the crowd.
s102.vr: Sunset on Nov 18 lights the cone orange from here; it is the frame the whole drive day points at.
s102.tk: on the drive day, 2 h by car
s102.ky: 2 h 30, Shinkansen to Shin-Fuji + 25 min taxi

s103.why: Fujinomiya yakisoba is the city's B-grade dish: firm steamed noodles, pork-fat crumbs, sardine powder, fried on a plate in front of you at stalls beside the Sengen shrine. Omiya Yokocho is the cluster, 10:00 to 17:00, pay parking by the river.
s103.only: Noodles you will not meet anywhere else, but it is a 30-minute detour on a day that already has Yoshida udon (s68) for lunch; one local noodle a day is enough.
s103.vr: Only if Nov 18 runs ahead of time between Asagiri and the tea fields; the sunset at Obuchi matters more.
s103.tk: on the drive day, 2 h by car
s103.ky: 2 h 15, Shinkansen to Shin-Fuji + Minobu line

s104.why: A six-minute walk from Ito station: oden simmered in chicken broth since 1961, kinmedai (the red snapper Izu is known for) grilled or simmered, and a flight of Shizuoka sakes. A local izakaya with no tourists and a counter where the owner talks.
s104.only: Kinmedai is Izu's fish and this is the night you are in Izu; Tokyo sushi counters sell it at three times the price. Marutaka nearby does uzuwa, the pounded frigate tuna with green chilli, if you want the stranger local dish.
s104.vr: Dinner on the Nov 18 Ito night after check-in at K's House; it is the honest end to the drive day.
s104.tk: on the drive day; 1 h 40 by Odoriko train otherwise
s104.ky: 3 h 30, Shinkansen to Atami + Ito line

s105.why: Lava cliffs where a Fuji-side volcano ran into the Pacific, a 48-metre suspension bridge swinging over the swell, a lighthouse you can climb, and a cliff path south if you want more. Twenty minutes from Ito, ¥500 car park, and at 06:25 on Nov 19 the sun comes up over the sea in front of you.
s105.only: The only ocean on the whole trip and the only sunrise you can reach by car from a bed; Enoshima (p03) is a tamer version of coast with a train. This is also the one dark-sky window of the trip, after the 00:16 moonset.
s105.vr: Sunrise over the Pacific before the Izu Skyline is the kind of morning you remember; it costs you an alarm, nothing else.
s105.tk: on the drive day; 2 h 10 by Odoriko + bus otherwise
s105.ky: 3 h 45, Shinkansen to Atami + Izu Kyuko line

s106.why: A bakery one minute from Ito station where commuters buy bread and coffee before work; you eat standing, with the town's day beginning around you. Sweet House Wakaba, a 1948 coffee house nearby, has the soft serve that locals swear by.
s106.only: Breakfast with locals rather than a hotel buffet; nothing special about the bread, everything about the room. If K's House breakfast is enough, skip it.
s106.vr: A ten-minute coffee after the Jogasaki sunrise before the Skyline; keep it loose.
s106.ky: 3 h 30, Shinkansen to Atami + Ito line

s107.why: The ridge road along Izu's spine: 40 km of sweeping bends with Fuji ahead, Sagami Bay on your right and Suruga Bay on your left, and the Sukumoyama pull-off where both appear at once. You drive the northern 30 km from the Kameishi gate to Atami pass, about ¥1,000 at the cashless gates.
s107.only: The best road on the trip for a Roadster with the roof down, better surfaced and emptier than the Hakone roads, and in late November the air is at its clearest. The Turnpike (s113) is the climb, the Skyline is the cruise.
s107.vr: This is what the MX-5 was rented for; the Nov 19 morning on the Skyline is the drive-day hero.
s107.tk: on the drive day, 2 h by car

s108.why: The pass named for the ten old provinces you can see from it: Fuji, both bays, the Hakone crater rim and on a clear day the Boso peninsula across Tokyo Bay. The car park already has most of the view; the cable car to the top adds ¥730 and a hundred metres.
s108.only: The widest panorama on the drive, wider than Daikanzan (s23) and higher than Jukkoku's neighbour Nagao Pass (s26); twenty minutes is enough unless you want the cable car.
s108.vr: On the Nov 19 route at 11:00 between the Skyline and the Hakone descent; costs nothing to stop.
s108.tk: on the drive day, 1 h 50 by car

s109.why: A bakery on the Lake Ashi shore at Motohakone where you eat lunch with your feet in a hot-spring foot bath facing the lake; the red torii of Hakone Shrine is five minutes along the shore for the photo. Pay lots at Motohakone-ko.
s109.only: The foot bath is the gimmick and it is a good one after a morning of driving; the bread is decent, not exceptional. For a proper Hakone lunch, soba at Hatsuhana in Yumoto is better food with no view.
s109.vr: Nov 19 lunch at 12:50 as planned; it fixes the torii photo and the lake in one stop.
s109.tk: on the drive day; 2 h 15 by Romancecar + bus otherwise

s110.why: A thatched tea house on the old Tokaido highway that has served walkers since the early 1600s: unsweetened koji amazake, chikara-mochi grilled over charcoal with soy or kinako, an open hearth and tatami. The same family, thirteen generations. Same place as the one on your list (p102).
s110.only: The oldest working business on the trip and the only piece of the Edo-period road you will sit inside; Asagiri's tea house (s101) is modern by comparison. Twenty-five minutes is right.
s110.vr: You asked for it, it is on the Nov 19 descent, and it costs ¥900; rate it under p102.
s110.tk: on the drive day; 2 h 30 by Romancecar + bus otherwise

s111.why: Outdoor hot-spring baths on the Haya river at Hakone Yumoto, several pools at different temperatures under trees, used by locals and Tokyo day-trippers, ¥1,450, towels for rent. An hour including the drive-in and out.
s111.only: The best day-onsen in Hakone and the only chance for an outdoor bath in nature on the trip (K's House is indoor); but it eats the hour you need to return the car by 18:30 in Adachi.
s111.vr: Only if the Nov 19 day runs early; a late car return costs ¥6,600 per 30 minutes, which is the price of three onsens.
s111.tk: on the drive day; 1 h 40 by Romancecar + 10 min bus otherwise
s111.ky: 3 h, Shinkansen to Odawara + Tozan line

s112.why: The decided car: a 2015 MX-5 ND 1.5 six-speed manual from OnlyJDM's Tokyo North store in Adachi, ¥17,000 a day plus cover, 200 km per 24 h and ¥55 a kilometre beyond. Pickup 10:00 Nov 18, return by 18:30 Nov 19; ten minutes on foot from Rokucho on the Tsukuba Express.
s112.only: The practical point: bring the physical Indian licence, the 1949-convention IDP and passport, expect the ¥50,000 deposit on card, and budget about 110 km of overage on the loop. No out-of-hours return.
s112.vr: Decided and built into the plan; this entry is here so the pickup and return get rated as part of the drive days.
s112.tk: 35 min, Tsukuba Express to Rokucho + 10 min walk

s113.why: The 13.8 km toll climb from Odawara to Daikanzan at 1,011 m: long sweeping bends, Sagami Bay opening up behind you, Fuji ahead near the top, a surface the car magazines test on. ¥900 at the gate, and the Mazda café (s65) at the summit.
s113.only: The Skyline (s107) is the cruise; this is the climb, the road where a manual Roadster earns its rental. It is also the quickest way off the Hakone plateau toward the Tomei when the day runs late.
s113.vr: You asked for it, it is on the Nov 19 afternoon, and it ends at the café where the car people are.
s113.tk: on the drive day, 1 h 15 by car to the Odawara gate

s114.why: A single room with a bath and a desk, 10 minutes from Tokyo station, for the one night between the car and the 07:00 Nozomi. Business hotels are the Japanese default: small, spotless, quiet.
s114.only: Practical: book a chain (Sotetsu Fresa Inn, APA, Dormy Inn) on its own site; cancellation is free until the day before.
s114.vr: You rated the CITAN dorm 1; a ¥10,000 single buys sleep before a 06:30 alarm.

s115.why: One night on tatami with a futon laid out for you, a wooden bath and a Japanese breakfast, in a small family-run ryokan near Kyoto station. The ryokan night you asked about, in the city where it belongs.
s115.only: Practical: Ryokan Shimizu and Nishiyama Ryokan are real family ryokan at ¥12,000–16,000, not hotel-style resorts; the holiday weekend is nearly sold out, so decide this week.
s115.vr: Worth it if you want the futon night; Len is fine if you would rather spend the ¥8,000 difference on the knife.

s116.why: Fuji snowmelt filters through lava for decades and comes out here as hundreds of thin white threads along a 150 m curved cliff, dropping into a pool that reads blue-white in sun. Ten minutes of steps down from the car park, then you stand at the water.
s116.only: The only waterfall on the drive and the clearest water on it; different from the lakes because the colour comes from the spring water itself, not depth. Easy: 30 min total.
s116.vr: On the way from Motosu to Ito, 30 minutes, free, and it is the blue water you asked for.
s116.tk: on the drive day; 2 h 30 by car

s117.why: A scruffy second-floor room packed with used LPs priced to move, most ¥500–1,500, run by a man who has done this since the 1980s. You flip crates; the rock, prog and soundtrack bins are deep.
s117.only: Only here: the cheapest serious vinyl in west Tokyo. Disk Union grades and prices higher; this is where a cheap Pink Floyd actually turns up. Closed Wednesdays, open Tuesday.
s117.vr: Settles your vinyl rule in 30 minutes, three minutes from the thrift shop.

s118.why: Jimbocho is Tokyo’s curry district: a hundred shops around the bookstores feed students and editors. Bondy’s European-style beef curry comes with a hot boiled potato and butter; Kyoeido has made its spiced Sumatra curry since 1924.
s118.only: Why it is special: this is the curry culture your own note calls the best in Japan, inside the book town you flagged can’t-miss, so lunch costs no travel. Better option nearby: Ethiopia or Gavial if the Bondy queue is over 30 min.
s118.vr: Free lunch slot inside a can’t-miss stop; the queue is the only cost.

s119.why: The open wooden balcony of Nigatsu-do hangs above Todai-ji and faces west across the whole Nara plain. At sunset the sky goes orange behind the Ikoma hills, the bronze lanterns come on, and the deer wander up the stone path below you.
s119.only: What makes it unique: the only free, unticketed sunset platform in Nara, open all hours, and it is 10 minutes from the Great Buddha you were visiting anyway.
s119.vr: Zero cost, on the way to the car, and it fixes the sunset for the Saturday.
s119.ky: 50 min, Kintetsu + walk; on the drive day

s120.why: A5 kuroge wagyu grilled piece by piece at the counter, from tongue to the fat-marbled cuts, with sauces that change per cut. Omakase courses ¥11,000–16,000; counter seats take solo diners.
s120.only: Why it is special: a yakiniku omakase is the way Japanese people eat 10/10 wagyu; the Blue Room on your list is a hotel dining room that happens to serve it. Better option: Yoroniku in Minami-Aoyama if you can get a seat.
s120.vr: The honest answer to “10/10 wagyu”, but it is a swap, not an addition: one big dinner is enough.

s121.why: A 1 h 45 session in a historic samurai residence in west-central Kyoto: you are dressed in samurai clothes, hear the history of the house, practise drawing and cutting form with a training sword, take your cuts at a target, sit Zen, and then handle antique swords. Staff photograph the sword part and send the pictures the same day. About ¥18,000.
s121.only: The best-reviewed sword session in Kyoto (4.97 from 655 on Airbnb, 5.0 from 1,498 on Viator). It uses a training sword: real-blade cutting for visitors ended in Kyoto after a police notice in December 2024. YAIBA KYOTO near Karasuma Oike is the cheaper, newer alternative built around draw-and-cut; HiSUi in Ginza (s74) is the one that may still hand you a live blade.
s121.vr: You found it yourself and gave up the Kurama walk for it. Friday Nov 20 at 10:00 is the only slot that fits your Kyoto days; one spot was left on Nov 11.
s121.ky: 15 min by taxi from Kyoto station
